rows.fidelity_note: Statement 2.1 expands Mathlib’s `RiemannHypothesis`, the exact type of the theorem in `Main.lean`. The variables, the exclusions $s=-2(n+1)$ and $s=1$, and the conclusion $\operatorname{Re}s=1/2$ agree.
rows.annotation: There is no hypothesis that $s$ belongs to the critical strip. For the unique character modulo $1$ the $L$-function is $\zeta$, so [Statement 2.2](pdf#theorem.2.2) excludes zeros to the right of $\tfrac12$, away from $1$. For a zero to the left, put $t=1-s$: then $\operatorname{Re}t>\tfrac12$ and $t\ne1$ since $\zeta(0)=-\tfrac12$. In the functional equation $\zeta(s)=2(2\pi)^{-t}\Gamma(t)\cos(\pi t/2)\zeta(t)$ the power, gamma and zeta factors are nonzero. Thus $t=3,5,7,\ldots$, the positive odd integers other than $1$, and $s=-2,-4,-6,\ldots$ are precisely the zeros excluded in the statement.

ties.fidelity_note: Statement 2.1 expands Mathlib’s `RiemannHypothesis`, the exact type of the theorem in `Main.lean`. The variables, the exclusions $s=-2(n+1)$ and $s=1$, and the conclusion $\operatorname{Re}s=1/2$ agree.

explanation.text: Where can the Riemann zeta function vanish? Its known zeros at $-2,-4,-6,\ldots$ are called trivial zeros. The point $s=1$ is a pole, where the meromorphic function blows up. The Riemann Hypothesis puts every other zero on the vertical line $\operatorname{Re}s=1/2$. The location matters for counting primes. In the smoothed count used in the paper, a zero $\rho$ contributes a term proportional to $x^\rho$. A zero farther to the right has a larger real part and gives a faster-growing term. Alpöge’s proof rules out zeros to the right of the line for all Dirichlet $L$-functions, including $\zeta$ at modulus one. The zeta functional equation rules out a remaining zero to the left by reflecting it to $1-s$.

rows.annotation: The modulus is positive (`NeZero N`), and $\chi=1$ denotes the principal character modulo $N$, whose $L$-function is $\zeta(s)\prod_{p\mid N}(1-p^{-s})$ away from $1$. The factors are nonzero at $1$, so the pole occurs for the principal character of every modulus; the disjunction excludes just that case and includes $s=1$ for non-principal characters. This is a statement about the meromorphic continuation (`LFunction`), not the Dirichlet series (`LSeries`); in Lean even at a pole the former is a complex-valued function. More generally, the change of modulus from the conductor to $N$ introduces factors $1-\psi(p)p^{-s}$, where $\psi$ is the inducing primitive character; as $|\psi(p)p^{-s}|\le p^{-\operatorname{Re}s}<1$ for $\operatorname{Re}s>0$, these introduce no zeros there. Hence the primitive non-vanishing assertion `ZeroFreeAll` of [Section 3](pdf#section.3) suffices.

explanation.text: A Dirichlet character weights the terms of the zeta series according to their residue classes. Every such character comes from a primitive character at its conductor, the smallest modulus that induces it. After proving nonvanishing at the primitive level, the argument uses a finite product to recover the $L$-function at the original modulus. Each extra factor has the form $1-\chi_*(p)p^{-s}$, where $\chi_*$ is the primitive character. For $\operatorname{Re}s>0$, the term subtracted from $1$ has modulus at most $p^{-\operatorname{Re}s}<1$, so these factors cannot introduce zeros in the half-plane of the theorem.

rows.annotation: Write $a=0$ or $1$ according as $\chi$ is even or odd. explanation.text: A primitive character is given at its conductor, so its functional equation can be applied without first removing Euler factors from a larger modulus. rows.annotation: `ZeroFreeAll` is non-vanishing in $\operatorname{Re}s>\tfrac12$ for primitive characters of every conductor and either parity. rows.name: Deduction.landau_window
rows.plain: Landau’s pole bound from window estimates
rows.note: The Lean split is between a pole closer to a shifted vertical center than the pole-free radius at the real center, and an isolated real pole inside a disk at the real center. Lean uses the norm of the residue in the shifted calculation and its positive real value in the real calculation.
rows.annotation: Write $g(v)=G_F(e^v)$ and $\Phi(s)=\int_0^\infty g(v)e^{-sv}\,dv$ for $\operatorname{Re}s>2$. The coefficient of $z^k$ in $\Phi(s-z)$ is $T_k(s)=\int_0^\infty g(v)v^ke^{-sv}\,dv/k!$. At a real $\sigma>2$, with $w_k(v)=v^ke^{-\sigma v}/k!$, the triangle inequality gives $|T_k(\sigma+it)|+\operatorname{Re}T_k(\sigma)\le 2\int_0^\infty\max(g(v),0)w_k(v)\,dv$. The additional real coefficient cancels the contribution of the negative part in the upper bound: one obtains an estimate at every height $t$ from an upper bound for $g$ alone, with no lower bound on the window.

rows.name: Deduction.lemmaL
rows.plain: Integrated window bounds imply nonvanishing for a character family
rows.note: `lemmaL` turns the abstract pole result into an $L$-function theorem. It constructs the family’s pole data, uses `landau_window` for zeros in $0<\operatorname{Re}s<1$, and applies the known nonvanishing theorem for the remaining region $\operatorname{Re}s\ge1$.
rows.annotation: The smoothing in [(4.1)](pdf#equation.4.1) gives $\int_{\log n}^\infty(e^v/n-1)e^{-sv}\,dv=n^{-s}/(s(s-1))$. For $\chi\ne1$ the resulting transform is $\bigl(-L'/L(s,\chi)+sL'/L(1,\chi)\bigr)/(s(s-1))$; the correction removes the apparent pole at $1$, and the zeta correction similarly removes its double and simple pole terms there. Taking real parts of $G_{\chi_i}(y)$ averages the transforms for $\chi_i$ and $\chi_i^{-1}$, so at a zero $\rho$ in the strip the family residue is $-S/(\rho(\rho-1))$, where $S=\sum_i a_i(m_i+m_i')/2$ and $m_i,m_i'$ are the orders of vanishing of the two functions at $\rho$. These orders are non-negative, and $S>0$ at any zero of a member: the residues cannot cancel, and at a real $0<\rho<1$ the residue is positive.

explanation.text: Write $v=\log y$ and $U=\log Y$. The multiplicative window becomes $[U,(1+\omega)U]$. The $k$th Laplace coefficient at a real center $\sigma$ weights the sum by $v^k e^{-\sigma v}/k!$, which peaks at $k/\sigma$. Choosing $k$ near $(1+\omega/2)\sigma U$ puts the peak in the middle of the window. The tail estimates and the upper bound on the window then limit the coefficient. An isolated pole at distance $d$ gives a term proportional to $d^{-k-1}$. The proof chooses the real or shifted center so this term grows faster relative to the bound as $k$ increases.

rows.note: `HostFactsS` records the ramification and Frobenius conditions for a host field used in the character-sum identity.
rows.annotation: Write $I_p$ for inertia at $p$: the character value at $p^i$ is the mean of $\psi$ on the coset $C_{p,i}=i\operatorname{Frob}_p+I_p$ (in additive notation), rather than its value at an arbitrary representative. rows.fidelity_note: `De` expands to the double sum in Statement 4.2. Lean permits any complex correction `ell`, which appears in both `MAIN` and the character sums. The paper uses logarithmic derivatives at $1$. The explicit integer cutoff $N$ can be chosen above all ratios $a/w(\rho)$, beyond which the count has zero weight.
rows.annotation: For fixed $g\notin\Phi$ put $W=w(\rho_g)$; the identity $W(a/(Wn)-1)_+=\max(a/n-W,0)$ gives the weight of the count from [(4.1)](pdf#equation.4.1). To recover the uncentred prime sum from $WG_\psi(a/W)$ one adds $a(\log a-1-\gamma-\log W)$ for $\psi=1$, and $-aL'/L(1,\psi)$ otherwise. The partner bijection averages $\log W$ over all of $\Phi$, while the mean of $\overline{\psi}(g)$ on the complementary coset is $1$ for $\psi=1$, $-1$ for $\psi=\chi_\Phi$, and zero for every other character; the latter cancellation applies to the non-trivial corrections because they no longer depend on $W$. This gives (4.4), including the plus sign of $aL'/L(1,\chi_\Phi)$, and makes MAIN independent of $t$ for fixed $a,w$. In Lean the identity holds with arbitrary `ell` in place of the logarithmic derivatives and an integer cutoff $N$ with $a/w(\rho)\le N$ for every $\rho\in\Phi$.

ties.fidelity_note: `De` expands to the double sum in Statement 4.2. Lean permits any complex correction `ell`, which appears in both `MAIN` and the character sums. The paper uses logarithmic derivatives at $1$. The explicit integer cutoff $N$ can be chosen above all ratios $a/w(\rho)$, beyond which the count has zero weight.

explanation.text: For an unramified prime power, the count first asks whether its Frobenius lies outside the subgroup $\Phi$. Each class outside $\Phi$ has a partner of weight $w$ that sets its cutoff $a/w$. Rewriting the test for that class by character orthogonality turns its prime-power sum into a linear combination of the $G_\psi$ at the same cutoff. Subtracting the explicit main term gives the identity. This is the point where an upper bound for the arithmetic count becomes an upper bound for a real part of a combination of analytic sums.

rows.name: Deduction.ch_balance
rows.plain: The exact count identity from character orthogonality
rows.note: `askExp` expands the weighted count and treats the exceptional ramified prime separately. After identifying `De`, `ch_balance` uses `colour_sum` to keep only the quotient character in the nontrivial correction to `MAIN`.
rows.annotation: Interchange the sums in `askExp` and fix $p^i$, with inertia group $I_p$ and coset $C_{p,i}=i\operatorname{Frob}_p+I_p$. With $\psi(p^i)$ read as the mean over this coset, orthogonality gives $|\Phi|^{-1}\sum_{\psi\in\widehat{\mathfrak G}}\overline{\psi}(g)\psi(p^i)=(2/|I_p|)\mathbf{1}_{g\in C_{p,i}}$: the factor two comes from $|\mathfrak G|=2|\Phi|$. At an unramified prime the coset is a singleton, giving the coefficient $2\log p$ after multiplication by $\Lambda(p^i)=\log p$; the condition $\chi_\Phi(\operatorname{Frob}_p)^i=-1$ selects exactly the odd powers of primes inert in the quadratic field fixed by $\Phi$; the partner weight still depends on the full Frobenius power. The series $1/p+1/p^3+\cdots$ of these reciprocal powers is the derivative gain per order at an inert prime in [Section 6.1](pdf#subsection.6.1), before the capacity and loss terms. If all weights were a common $W$, the character average on the complement would give $\mathrm{ASK}-\mathrm{MAIN}=W(G(a/W)-G_{\chi_\Phi}(a/W))$. The variable weights in Statement 4.2 instead allow other characters to occur: under its size and character hypotheses, [Statement 4.3](pdf#theorem.4.3) turns an upper bound for the sum of the real deviations at each translate into a bound for the kept sum, with an error for the omitted characters.

explanation.text: Fix a group element $g$ outside $\Phi$ and an unramified prime power with Frobenius $f$. In the sum over characters, $\overline{\psi(g)}\psi(f)$ equals $1$ for every $\psi$ when $f=g$. When $f\ne g$, the character values sum to zero. Dividing by the group order therefore gives the indicator of $f=g$, which is the test the weighted count needs. At a ramified prime, the same operation is averaged over the inertia coset. The identity uses the full character sum before later steps estimate or drop any contributions.

rows.annotation: For fixed $a_t$ the quantity to be approximated is $wG_\psi(a_t/w)$, not $G_\psi(a_t/w)$ alone. The resulting term has the same weight at every lift, and its argument is $a_t/b$, still to be moved to $x$.

explanation.text: At a thick place, the weight is close to $b$ and $a_t/b$ is within 1 of $x$, so this part of the sum can be moved to the target scale. At a thin place, the smaller weight sends the sum to a much larger scale. The last clause bounds $a_t/w$ by the finite cutoff used in the count.

rows.name: Deduction.ch_core
rows.plain: A near-square-root bound for the kept characters’ weighted sum
rows.note: Lean first moves each evaluation from $a_t/b$ to $x$, then estimates the character coefficient. It uses the prescribed average for kept characters nontrivial on $H$ and the exact coefficient $1$ for those trivial on $H$. For omitted characters the estimate contributes their norms at $x$ plus the movement error. A one-character estimate is summed over the top places and rearranged into the kept sum and its absolute-value error.
rows.annotation: For a kept character put $c_\psi=|TT|^{-1}\sum_{t\in TT}\psi(0,t)$. Since $\psi(\sigma)=1$, replacing the arguments $a_t/b$ by $x$ in the mean leaves $c_\psi G_\psi(x)$, with error $O(\log x)$ by (2) and the integrated derivative bound (only $O(1)$ for $\psi=1$). If $\psi$ is trivial on $H$ then $c_\psi=1$ exactly; otherwise $|c_\psi-\beta|\le Mx^{-1+\varepsilon}$, and the bound $|G_\psi(x)|\ll x\log x$ for non-trivial kept characters suffices to make the error in replacing $c_\psi$ by $\beta$ at most $O(x^\varepsilon\log x)$, with no square-root estimate assumed. For an omitted character the phase has modulus one, so the real mean is at least $-|G_\psi(x)|-O(\log x)$. As at most $M$ characters remain, these errors are $o(x^{1/2+\varepsilon})$ in total and the real mean is at least $G_{\mathcal K'}(x)-\Sigma_{\mathcal K'}(x)-4x^{1/2+\varepsilon}$.

explanation.text: To see how a weight emerges, take one kept character and add and subtract its value at the common evaluation point $x$ in every summand. One error comes from replacing $G_\psi(a_t/b)$ by $G_\psi(x)$, small because $|a_t/b-x|\le1$. Factoring out $G_\psi(x)$ leaves the sum of the character values over the set of sizes $TT$. Condition (1) makes this coefficient close to $\beta|TT|$ when the character is nontrivial on $H$. A character trivial on $H$ has coefficient exactly $|TT|$. Each omitted term has real part bounded below by the negative of its absolute value. This gives a lower bound for the full average in terms of the kept sum, which is how an upper bound on the average controls that sum.

rows.plain: A near-square-root bound from the size and error inequalities
rows.note: `GrowthSizeBound` names an implication between real inequalities. The input `Gx` is a real number.
rows.annotation: The leading part of the first bracket term is independent of $m$ for fixed $a_E,TT$; the second contains $m^2$. After division by $m$ their scales are $x/m$ and $m$, whose product is $x$: the model expression $x/m+m$ is least at $m=\sqrt{x}$, and the third cost is bounded separately by the upper bound on $k$. In the prescribed interval $x^{1/2-\varepsilon}\le m\le x^{1/2+\varepsilon/2}$ the largest exponent in the three upper bounds is $1/2+21\varepsilon/8$, from the second term: $\varepsilon/2$ from $m$, $\varepsilon$ from the explicit power, and $\varepsilon/8+\varepsilon$ from the two density factors. Division in [(4.5)](pdf#equation.4.5), with its factor $1/2$ and both additive errors retained, gives $G_{\mathcal K'}(x)-\Sigma_{\mathcal K'}(x)\le26x^{1/2+(C+21/8)\varepsilon}$; the condition $26\le x^{3\varepsilon/8}$ gives the stated exponent. This is the implication of `GrowthSizeBound`, proved by `proposition_size_bound`.

explanation.text: Take `Gx` to be the kept character sum minus the sum of absolute values of the discarded terms. Given the size conditions and the inequality before division, the conclusion is $\mathrm{Gx}\le x^{1/2+(C+3)\varepsilon}$. The paper’s earlier calculation explains why choosing $m$ near $\sqrt{x}$ gives this exponent.

ties.plain: Forms invariant under the genus stabilisers

rows.name: GlobalTheory.Mem.Col2.GStep.Fi
rows.plain: Forms invariant under the genus stabilisers
rows.note: The space underlying $M_u$ consists of weight-representation-valued functions on the finitely many genus classes. At each class the value must be fixed by that class’s stabiliser.
rows.annotation: For a genus class $c$, let $V_c$ be the subspace of the complex weight representation fixed by the stabiliser of $c$ (with its character action). The choices of a value at different classes are independent, so `Fi` is the product of the $V_c$ and has dimension $\sum_c\dim V_c$. In particular, when the stabilisers are trivial, the rank of the integral lattice $M_u$ is the number of classes times the dimension of the weight representation. It is this full rank that is used in the choice of the level $T(u)$; a space cut out by prescribed Hecke eigenvalues would not have this dimension formula.

ties.name: Formalism.BasicNotions.DV.Iu
ties.plain: The fractional ideal for the modified lattice

rows.name: Formalism.BasicNotions.DV.Iu
rows.plain: The fractional ideal for the modified lattice
rows.note: The fractional ideal rescales the ramified lattice one prime at a time. At $\lambda$ the exponent is $-\lfloor e_\lambda g(u,\lambda)\rfloor$, the negative of the valuation threshold for periods.
rows.annotation: Write $n_\lambda=\lfloor e_\lambda g(u,\lambda)\rfloor$. Locally the fractional ideal $I_u$ allows scalars of valuation at least $-n_\lambda$. With the infinite-place metrics unchanged, increasing $n_\lambda$ by one in a rank-$r$ lattice subtracts $r\log N\lambda$ from its log covolume, and hence adds $2\log N\lambda/[K:\mathbb Q]$ to its slope in the normalisation of Section 5.1. The rescaling is admissible because [Section 5.3](pdf#subsection.5.3) proves that the periods before rescaling have valuation at least $n_\lambda$ when nonzero; this also explains why a negative $n_\lambda$ is allowed.

ties.name: Formalism.BasicNotions.DV.NprimeDef
ties.plain: The modified lattice is scaled by the fractional ideal

rows.name: Formalism.BasicNotions.DV.NprimeDef
rows.plain: The modified lattice is scaled by the fractional ideal
rows.note: The lattice $N_u$ is generated by products of a scalar from the fractional ideal and a form from the sublattice ramified at $T(u)$. The admissibility bound allows those products to have integral periods even when the scalar introduces a denominator.
rows.annotation: There are two integral modules on the space of forms ramified at $T(u)$. The pullback of $M_u$ to that space is `MramL`; the module chosen before rescaling is `NuLat`. Away from $T(u)$, the latter is locally contained in the former, and agrees with it at dropped primes and at primes outside the inert and signal classes. If $L_u^0$ denotes `NuLat`, then `NprimeDef` says that the underlying module of $N_u$ is $I_uL_u^0$, the $\mathcal O_K$-span of all products of a scalar in $I_u$ and a form in $L_u^0$. Thus neither restriction to the ramified space alone nor multiplication of the whole $M_u$ by $I_u$ describes the lattice in (5.1).

ties.name: Formalism.BasicNotions.SizeData₂.sg
ties.plain: Sum of local gains and signed corrections across lifts

rows.name: Formalism.BasicNotions.SizeData₂.sg
rows.plain: Sum of local gains and signed corrections across lifts
rows.note: The real number $g(u,\lambda)$ adds the gains from the individual lifts, adds their first corrections, and subtracts their word-dependent corrections. Multiplication by the ramification index and rounding down turn this sum into the local valuation threshold.
rows.annotation: For fixed $\lambda$ only the second correction $\mathrm{ee}_j(u,\lambda)$ depends on the word $u$. If the rational prime below $\lambda$ is dropped, `gainD` sets the gain to zero, not the two corrections. The ramification factor converts the sum of all $m$ contributions into the local valuation units; taking the negative floor then changes $-e_\lambda g(u,\lambda)$ by a number in $[0,1)$. Thus the rounding costs less than one valuation unit at each supported place, independently of the number of lifts, and there is no truncation at zero.

ties.name: Formalism.LFunctionChainParameters.LChain.SizeData₂
ties.plain: The eleven lattice size conditions

rows.name: Formalism.LFunctionChainParameters.LChain.SizeData₂
rows.plain: The eleven lattice size conditions
rows.note: `SizeData₂` is a proposition on the slope data, constants and an auxiliary bound. Lines 17–19 list the eleven predicates side by side. In particular, `QuotientSlopeBoundsWith`, `LossBounds`, `SlopeIneq` and `DIV` supply the four displayed inequalities. `ChainTied` separately identifies the data’s scale with $x$ and requires all eleven predicates at line 109. This predicate is the conjunction of the eleven size clauses used by ChainTied.
rows.annotation: Fix $u_0$. The count $\mathrm{ASK}(u_0)$ and the gain $\mathrm{Ga}(u_0)$ are already single numbers; it is the slopes $\mu(N_u)-h(u)$, not the counts, that are averaged over $u$, with weights $\operatorname{rk}N_u$. The four displayed inequalities compare this mean with the common target slope $\mu(P)$ and the period bound. In the full record (Gain) also bounds $\mu_{\max}(N_u)$ from above, to control the error in (Slope), and (Loss) bounds the auxiliary index loss that enters $\mathrm{Lo}_5(u)$. The four closing clauses and the three positivity and size clauses make these comparisons effective at each translate, as required by condition (3) of [Statement 4.3](pdf#theorem.4.3).

explanation.text: For each translate, the proof passes from the prime-power count to the slopes of rescaled lattices of forms, then to the slope of their common period lattice. Divisibility allows the rescaled forms to map into that lattice. The period estimate supplies an upper bound on the same slope that the frame argument bounds from below. To remove the terms in between, the proof bounds the slopes of the original lattices, compares the map heights together with their level terms, counts forms to bound the level prime, and compares the rescaling correction with the host’s level primes. Positivity and size bounds make the resulting errors uniform over the translates. This is how the count is bounded by the analytic main term plus an error before applying the analytic reduction.

ties.name: Formalism.BasicNotions.SizeData₂.Ga
ties.plain: Total finite-place gain after penalties

rows.name: Formalism.BasicNotions.SizeData₂.Ga
rows.plain: Total finite-place gain after penalties
rows.note: At each place the argument sums the gains of the lifts and subtracts the local cost $\tau_\lambda$. The place-weighted total $\mathrm{Ga}(u_0)$ is the common quantity in the count bound and the lower slope bound for $N_u$.
rows.annotation: For a quantity $y$ in the units of $g(u,\lambda)$, the conversion to slope units is $2e_\lambda y\log N\lambda/[K:\mathbb Q]$ (`sz`). Over all places above a rational prime $p$ the coefficients of $y$ sum to $2\log p$, since $\log N\lambda=f_\lambda\log p$ and $\sum_{\lambda\mid p}e_\lambda f_\lambda=[K:\mathbb Q]$. This is the normalisation of the unramified-prime [count (4.3)](pdf#equation.4.3). The sum in $\mathrm{Ga}$ is over the finite support and deducts $\tau_\lambda$ once per place, after summing over the lifts: consequently $\mathrm{Ga}+\mathrm{Fo}-\mathrm{Ee}(u)=\sum_\lambda\mathrm{sz}_\lambda(g(u,\lambda)-\tau_\lambda)$ before rounding, with the further index losses accounted for in (Gain).

ties.name: Formalism.BasicNotions.SizeData₂.Fo
ties.plain: Sum the finite-place costs

rows.name: Formalism.BasicNotions.SizeData₂.Fo
rows.plain: Sum the finite-place costs
rows.note: $\mathrm{Fo}$ collects the word-independent rescaling corrections over the lifts and finite places. Subtracting it in the period inequality cancels the contribution it makes to the lower slope bound for $N_u$.
rows.annotation: The correction $\mathrm{Fo}$ is independent of $u$ at the fixed translate. Subtract (Div) from (Gain), writing $D(u)$ for the entire right side of (Div): one obtains $\mu(N_u)-h(u)-\mu(P)\ge\mu(M_u)+\mathrm{Ga}(u_0)-\mathrm{Ee}(u)-\mathrm{Lo}_5(u)-D(u)$. The height-adjusted slope on the left is precisely the quantity to be averaged in (Slope). The two occurrences of $\mathrm{Fo}$ have disappeared already, without any bound on their size.

ties.name: Formalism.BasicNotions.SizeData₂.Ee
ties.plain: Sum the losses for one word

rows.name: Formalism.BasicNotions.SizeData₂.Ee
rows.plain: Sum the losses for one word
rows.note: $\mathrm{Ee}(u)$ collects the word-dependent corrections and is subtracted in the lower bound for $\mu(N_u)$. The dimension count for $T(u)$ gives another occurrence of its leading term, which can then be cancelled.
rows.annotation: For each lift $j$, the finite-place sum of $\mathrm{ee}_j(u,\lambda)$ is compared with $\ell_g\sum_t a_t$, where $\ell_g$ is the logarithm of the product of the two fixed auxiliary level primes of the host, not the word-dependent prime $T(u)$. Adding the $m$ comparisons gives $\mathrm{Ee}(u)=m\ell_g\sum_t a_t$ up to $c_E mB_0$. The quantity to be controlled is the difference from this common leading term, not the absolute size of $\mathrm{Ee}(u)$, and the comparison holds for every word separately.

ties.name: Formalism.RankGapBounds.WeightedMeanData.Data.Slopes
ties.plain: Lower and upper bounds for lattice slopes

rows.name: Formalism.RankGapBounds.WeightedMeanData.Data.Slopes
rows.plain: Lower and upper bounds for lattice slopes
rows.note: The lower bound on the average slope of $M_u$ limits how much the starting lattice can cost in the gain inequality. The upper bound on its maximal slope separately controls the highest part of its Harder–Narasimhan filtration.
rows.annotation: The lower bound for $\mu(M_u)$ goes into (Gain). To use [Statement 5.1](pdf#theorem.5.1) one must also control $u_F=\max_u(\mu_{\max}(N_u)-h(u))-\bar\mu$, the excess of the largest adjusted slope in the whole family over its mean. In comparing $\mu_{\max}(N_u)-h(u)$ with $\mu(N_{u'})-h(u')$, the upper and lower rescaling bounds cancel $\mathrm{Ga}$ and $\mathrm{Fo}$: what remains is the difference $\mu_{\max}(M_u)-\mu(M_{u'})$, the difference of $-\mathrm{Ee}-h$ between the two words, and the errors in rescaling. Taking the rank-weighted mean over $u'$ and then the maximum over $u$ gives the desired bound; this is why the maximal-slope bound in `Slopes` is needed as well as the mean-slope bound.

ties.name: Formalism.RankGapBounds.WeightedMeanData.Data.HComp
ties.plain: Variation in adjusted map heights across words

rows.name: Formalism.RankGapBounds.WeightedMeanData.Data.HComp
rows.plain: Variation in adjusted map heights across words
rows.note: Two words in the same translate can have different map heights and different auxiliary level primes. The bound controls the variation of their combined quantity $h(u)+\sum_t a_t\log T(u)$, which appears when the level term is brought to the same side as the height.
rows.annotation: Put $A=\sum_t a_t$ and $H_u=h(u)+A\log T(u)$, where $h(u)$ is the chosen height bound. This is the height bound with the negative level contribution in (Div) added back. The clause `HComp` controls $|H_u-H_{u'}|$; to recover the variation of $h$ itself use $h(u)-h(u')=H_u-H_{u'}-A\log(T(u)/T(u'))$. The last inequality of `Count5` therefore gives an additional cost at most $Ac_{\mathrm{Count}}\log k$ in the comparison of adjusted slopes.

ties.name: Formalism.LFunctionChainParameters.WeightedSlopeBounds.Count5
ties.plain: Bounds on the period index and its variation across words

rows.name: Formalism.LFunctionChainParameters.WeightedSlopeBounds.Count5
rows.plain: Bounds on the period index and its variation across words
rows.note: The dimension count forces a lower bound on $\log T(u)$. Since the period bound contains $-\sum_t a_t\log T(u)$, this lower bound gives an upper bound on that contribution.
rows.annotation: For fixed $u_0$ the lower bound for $\log T(u)$ in `Count5` is independent of $u$, since the weights $w_j(\rho)$ are fixed. With $A=\sum_t a_t\ge0$, it gives an upper bound for the term $-A\log T(u)$ in (Div), in particular the term $-m\ell_g A$. The upper bound $\log T(u)\le c_{\mathrm{Count}}mL$ is needed instead in $\mathrm{Lo}_5(u)$, where the coefficient of $\log T(u)$ is $c_{\mathrm{Sl1}}|TT|m(a/k+b')$. Finally, the difference of the logarithms at two words is bounded by $c_{\mathrm{Count}}\log k$, so the estimate for $h(u)+A\log T(u)$ controls the variation of $h(u)$ as well.

ties.name: Formalism.LFunctionChainParameters.WeightedSlopeBounds.EComp5
ties.plain: Approximate the losses by the lift scalar term

rows.name: Formalism.LFunctionChainParameters.WeightedSlopeBounds.EComp5
rows.plain: Approximate the losses by the lift scalar term
rows.note: The correction $\mathrm{Ee}(u)$ differs from $m\ell_g\sum_t a_t$ by a controlled error. The same leading term, with a minus sign, appears when the lower bound on $\log T(u)$ is inserted into the period inequality.
rows.annotation: In the upper bound for the gain obtained by combining (Gain) and (Div), the level-dependent terms are $\mathrm{Ee}(u)-A\log T(u)$, with $A=\sum_t a_t$. Write $\mathrm{Ee}(u)=m\ell_gA+r(u)$ and the lower bound for $\log T(u)$ as $L_0+m\ell_g$, where $L_0$ is the weight term less the counting error. Then $\mathrm{Ee}(u)-A\log T(u)\le r(u)-AL_0$. [Statement 5.2](pdf#theorem.5.2) identifies the remaining period expression with the analytic main term plus the counting error, and `EComp5` bounds $|r(u)|$ by $c_E mB_0$; no smallness of $m\ell_g A$ is required. The same error bound gives $|\mathrm{Ee}(u)-\mathrm{Ee}(u')|\le2c_E mB_0$ in the estimate for $u_F$.

ties.name: Formalism.MainNotions.LocalQuadraticParts.adm2
ties.plain: Local divisibility of pairings of integral forms

rows.name: Formalism.MainNotions.LocalQuadraticParts.adm2
rows.plain: Local divisibility of pairings of integral forms
rows.note: For a form in the unscaled lattice and an allowed integral test vector, a nonzero period has valuation at least $\lfloor e_\lambda g(u,\lambda)\rfloor$ at $\lambda$. That is the threshold needed to multiply the form by the rescaling ideal while keeping its periods integral.
rows.annotation: It is the period of the rescaled form that must be integral, not the form in the original lattice. Put $k_\lambda=\lfloor e_\lambda g(u,\lambda)\rfloor$; the period of an unscaled form belongs to $\mathfrak P_\lambda^{k_\lambda}$ locally, so multiplication by the factor $\mathfrak P_\lambda^{-k_\lambda}$ of [(5.1)](pdf#equation.5.1) leaves the pairing integral. The test vectors used at $\lambda$ give the pairings with the local generators of $R$; checking them at every finite place puts the image in $R^\vee=P$.

ties.name: Formalism.L2.G.Adm2InU.admissible_level_two
ties.plain: Level-two divisibility and its complementary bound

rows.name: Formalism.L2.G.Adm2InU.admissible_level_two
rows.plain: Level-two divisibility and its complementary bound
rows.note: The proof establishes the valuation threshold separately at the auxiliary level prime $T(u)$, at the two host primes, and at the remaining places. These local bounds make the period map integral on $N_u$.
rows.annotation: Away from $T(u)$ and the two host level primes, the last column of the lift is $cz$, with $z$ in the localised integral lattice and $v_\lambda(c)\ge e_\lambda(g(u,\lambda)+\Delta)$ when the period is nonzero. The period of $z$ has valuation at least $-e_\lambda\Delta$, where $\Delta$ is the denominator term `vDG`; the two terms in $\Delta$ cancel, giving the unrounded bound. At $T(u)$ the denominator term vanishes by coprimality, and at the two host primes the proof uses a separate bound and clears a local unit. The other conclusion of `admissible_level_two` applies off $T(u)$ to the larger ramified lattice before the orbit restrictions: the bound there has $\sum_j(\mathrm{fo}_j-\mathrm{ee}_j)$ in place of $g(u,\lambda)$, without the gain.

ties.name: Formalism.MainNotions.G.gainP
ties.plain: The explicit gain at a prime

rows.name: Formalism.MainNotions.G.gainP
rows.plain: The explicit gain at a prime
rows.note: The local gain vanishes above the prime cutoff and at inert primes with $h_p=0$. In the orbit sum, each orbit contributes $\max(g_0,0)$, with $g_U-\mathrm{Pr}$ also included in the maximum on the orbits in $VV$.
rows.annotation: On an orbit in $VV$ write $A_j=\max(g_0,0)$ and $\Delta_j=\max(g_U-\mathrm{Pr}-A_j,0)$ for lift $j$; its contribution is $A_j+\Delta_j$, and on the other orbits it is just $A_j$. In forming the local sublattice `NP` one may apply the orbit's Hecke operator $m$ times, or omit it and multiply by $p^{\lceil\sum_j\Delta_j\rceil}$ instead (`Sv`). The latter supplies the extra divisibility without the operator. The required gain and the compensation powers are the same for all words at fixed translate, sizes and weights; the lattices themselves and the correction $\mathrm{ee}_j(u,\lambda)$ in the exponent may change with the word.

ties.name: Formalism.MainNotions.G.IsV
ties.plain: Even positions in the inert-prime orbit

rows.name: Formalism.MainNotions.G.IsV
rows.plain: Even positions in the inert-prime orbit
rows.note: At an inert prime the parity is measured by counting Frobenius steps from the chosen base point. The formula for $g_U$ charges the capacity deductions only at odd positions.
rows.annotation: Write $n'=\operatorname{ord}(h_p)$ at a prime of the inert class. The dropped primes and the zero-gain case $h_p=0$ leave only cycles of even length, so an odd step $e$ changes the parity of the position $i$ measured from the base point. The parity also enters the local lattice model: `lamAt` uses the given weight at even positions and its negative in reverse order (the dual weight) at odd positions. In (5.2) it is the parity of the starting position, not the already odd exponent $e$, that determines whether a capacity is deducted in $g_U$.

ties.name: Formalism.MainNotions.G.capU
ties.plain: Orbit capacity from the partner’s weight

rows.name: Formalism.MainNotions.G.capU
rows.plain: Orbit capacity from the partner’s weight
rows.note: The capacity is the adjusted weight at the partner reached after $e$ Frobenius steps, on the second copy for odd steps in the signal class. It caps the odd-position deduction in $g_U$ and is subtracted before taking the positive part in $g_0$.
rows.annotation: The first copy contains the top places; the second contains the thick set of this local model. For odd $e$ the partner lies on the second copy at a prime of the signal class, and on the first at a prime of the inert class. If $w_j$ is the weight at that partner, the formula actually uses $c_t(e)=w_j-\mathrm{kaJ}(j)+c_G$ and $\alpha_t=a_t-2c_G$. Thus the weight tested against $\alpha_t/p^e$ is not the weight at $t$, nor exactly the weight in the analytic count.

ties.name: Formalism.MainNotions.G.gU
ties.plain: Orbit gain after subtracting capped contributions

rows.name: Formalism.MainNotions.G.gU
rows.plain: Orbit gain after subtracting capped contributions
rows.note: On a single orbit, $g_U$ starts at $\gamma_p$ times the sum of the reduced top weights. It subtracts the capacity-limited terms at odd positions and an orbit error, leaving the full geometric-series contribution at even positions before that error.
rows.annotation: Put $z=\alpha_t/p^e$ for an odd exponent. If it is not excluded, the extra contribution of $g_U$ over $g_0$ at an even position is $z-\max(z-c_t(e),0)=\min(z,c_t(e))$; at an odd position it is zero. An excluded exponent contributes nothing to $g_0$ but still contributes $z$ or $\max(z-c_t(e),0)$ to $g_U$, respectively. The common orbit correction cancels from this difference, whereas $\mathrm{Pr}$ is still to be paid; the rate $\gamma_p$ itself comes from the factorial valuation less the formal logarithm loss in [Section 6.1](pdf#subsection.6.1).

ties.name: Formalism.MainNotions.G.g0
ties.plain: Orbit gain above the cap

rows.name: Formalism.MainNotions.G.g0
rows.plain: Orbit gain above the cap
rows.note: For each top place and each allowed odd exponent, $g_0$ counts only the positive excess of $\alpha_t/p^e$ over the partner capacity. The orbit’s logarithmic correction is then subtracted from the sum.
rows.annotation: The uncorrected summand of $g_0$ has the positive-part form of the [count (4.3)](pdf#equation.4.3), but with $\alpha_t$ and $c_t(e)$ in place of $a_t$ and the partner weight, and with first arrivals omitted. These changes need not all decrease the summand: in particular the capacity is an adjusted weight. The inequality actually used in (Loss), in `LinkG_at`, bounds the count on the retained top places, summed over the lifts and less the error terms, by $\sum_j\mathrm{gain}_j(\lambda)-\tau_\lambda$; the other top places and primes are accounted for by the loss estimate. It is not a termwise equality between $g_0$ and the count.

ties.name: Formalism.MainNotions.G.Excl
ties.plain: Odd first arrivals at a different top place

rows.name: Formalism.MainNotions.G.Excl
rows.plain: Odd first arrivals at a different top place
rows.note: An odd step is excluded from $g_0$ when it is the first positive step to a different top place on the first copy of the orbit.
rows.annotation: Suppose $t+h_p$ is another top place of an inert orbit of even length $n'$. The exponent $1$ is excluded, but $1+n'$ is not, although both are odd and have the same partner: only the least positive arrival at a different top place on the first copy is excluded. Consequently at an inert prime there is at most one excluded exponent per other top place of the orbit, while at a signal prime no odd exponent is excluded, since the partner is on the second copy.

ties.name: Formalism.MainNotions.G.VV
ties.plain: Eligible orbits at a candidate inert prime

rows.name: Formalism.MainNotions.G.VV
rows.plain: Eligible orbits at a candidate inert prime
rows.note: An orbit can use the $g_U$ estimate after its penalty only if it belongs to $VV$. To include the regular orbits, the construction requires a candidate inert prime, orbit length at least $x^{\epsilon/4}$, and a smallness bound summed over the regular orbits.
rows.annotation: At a candidate prime put $\sigma_p=m\sum_{t_0}\kappa_{t_0}$, the sum of `kapv` over the regular orbit representatives multiplied by the number of lifts. Either all these orbits enter $VV$, when $\sigma_p\le x^{-\epsilon}$, or none does. Besides the imposed restriction by $p^{\lceil\tau_p\rceil}$, the local index estimate has a further cost `ioP`, equal for nonempty $VV$ to $2\sigma_p\max_{t_0\in VV}\mathrm{Sv}(t_0)\le2x^{-\epsilon}\max_{t_0\in VV}\mathrm{Sv}(t_0)$; `LinkG_at` bounds the normalised colength off $T(u)$ by the rank times $\tau_\lambda+\mathrm{io}_\lambda$. It is $\tau_\lambda$ that is subtracted once in $\mathrm{Ga}$, not in the exponent $g(u,\lambda)$; the further index cost is controlled separately.

ties.name: Formalism.MainNotions.G.Good
ties.plain: Orbits satisfying the required top-position bounds

rows.name: Formalism.MainNotions.G.Good
rows.plain: Orbits satisfying the required top-position bounds
rows.note: The test constrains where the top places sit around one Frobenius orbit. It bounds their number in short windows and requires regularly recurring blocks with one even-position top place in every even cell and none in the odd cells.
rows.annotation: This is a condition on the set of positions, before the sizes and weights are chosen for the numerical test. In `IsGoodOrbit` the numbers of top places in cyclic windows of lengths $L_2$ and $G'$ are bounded by $K_G$ and $N_1$, respectively; in addition, divide the orbit from its base point into complete blocks of $(6r+1)U$ positions, with $U=\lceil1/\delta_1\rceil$ and $r=r_G$. From each block one finds, within the prescribed number of blocks (read cyclically), one whose odd-numbered cells of length $U$ are empty and whose even-numbered cells each contain exactly one top place, at an even position. This gives a run of $3r$ consecutive top places of even position, separated by more than $U$ steps; it does not require all top places of the orbit to be even.

ties.plain: Lower bound on the target lattice’s slope from a near-tight frame

rows.name: Formalism.HN.TheoremF
rows.plain: Lower bound on the target lattice’s slope from a near-tight frame
rows.fidelity_note: Lean’s `cc` is the lattice $P$, and its reference slope `s` satisfies the paper’s rank-weighted inequality for $\bar\mu$. The `Sum.inl` rows of `Ball` represent the original map in the chosen bases. The remaining rows take values in the added summand and count toward the codimension bound. Lean makes the positive total source rank and the nonnegativity of $e_F$ and $\eta_F$ explicit. It writes the conclusion as one formula, which gives zero for the logarithmic term at $u_F=0$ under Lean’s real division convention.
rows.annotation: The two frame bounds are used to compare ranks at one infinite place, not slopes. If a cut discards a fraction $r$ of the total source rank, let $U$ be the orthogonal complement of the span of the retained images in $W'_v$, put $z=\dim U/\dim W'_v$, and let $\operatorname{tr}_U Q$ be the trace of the compression of $Q$ to $U$. Only discarded source directions can contribute to this trace: the first bound, by Cauchy–Schwarz, gives $\operatorname{tr}_U Q/\operatorname{tr}Q\le(r+\sqrt{e_Fr})/(1-\sqrt{e_F})$, while the second gives $z-\sqrt{\eta_F z}\le\operatorname{tr}_U Q/\operatorname{tr}Q$ by subtracting the scalar part of $Q$. In particular, for $e_F=\eta_F=0$ one has $z\le r$; using $e_F\le1/4$ and $2\sqrt{\eta_F z}\le\eta_F+z$ gives $z\le\eta_F+4r+4\sqrt{e_F}$ in general. Projection onto the original rows of `Ball` (indexed by `Sum.inl`) cannot increase the absolute codimension; division by $\dim W_v\ge(1-\delta_F)\dim W'_v$ accounts for the enlargement factor. The ranks over $K$ can be read at $v$ in any bases, irrespective of the lattice metrics. [Section 7](pdf#section.7) supplies the frame bounds for the period maps.

The `Sum.inl` rows of `Ball` represent the original map in the chosen bases. The remaining rows take values in the added summand and count toward the codimension bound. explanation.text: Rescaling the source lattices raises their slopes. The proof needs that gain to reach the period lattice $P$, even though some of the maps may cover the same directions. At one infinite place, the Hilbert–Schmidt bound controls how far the weighted maps are from isometries, and the trace bound controls how unevenly their images cover the enlarged target. Cut each source at slope $\bar\mu-\tau+h_i$. The usual slope inequality places the surviving images in the part of $P$ of slope at least $\bar\mu-\tau$. The frame estimates bound the rank that can be missing there. Integrating over $0\le\tau\le HH$ gives the logarithmic error in the lower bound for the mean slope of $P$.

ties.plain: Bound the rank lost at a filtration cut

rows.name: Formalism.HN.frameB_share
rows.plain: Bound the rank lost at a filtration cut
rows.note: `frameB_share` bounds the count strictly below the cut when $u>0$. `TheoremF` applies it to height-adjusted slope lists, converts the count to lost rank, and handles $u=0$ separately. The conclusion bounds the fraction of slopes below the threshold by u divided by u plus tau.
rows.annotation: Count each slope $\lambda$ of $N_i$ with its rank multiplicity. Its deficit from the common upper bound, $\bar\mu+u_F-(\lambda-h_i)$, is non-negative, and the mean hypothesis bounds the sum of all these deficits by $u_F\sum_i\mathrm{rk}\,N_i$. Each slope cut away contributes more than $u_F+\tau$ to that sum, so the fraction cut away is at most $u_F/(u_F+\tau)$ for $u_F>0$; for $u_F=0$ all the adjusted slopes equal $\bar\mu$ and no rank is lost, even at $\tau=0$. Write $N_i(\tau)$ for the step retained at slope $\bar\mu-\tau+h_i$ (including equality). The minimum-slope inequality gives $\mu_{\min}(B_i(N_i(\tau)))\ge\mu_{\min}(N_i(\tau))-h_i\ge\bar\mu-\tau$ when the image is non-zero, so it lies in the step of $P$ of slope $\bar\mu-\tau$; the zero image lies there too. The frame estimate then bounds the rank of the sum of these images, which is a lower bound for the rank of that step of $P$.

explanation.text: Count a slope once for each rank it represents. After the height adjustment, their average is at least $\bar\mu$ and each slope is at most $\bar\mu+u_F$. Compare every slope to that upper limit. The average shortfall is at most $u_F$, while every slope below $\bar\mu-\tau$ uses at least $u_F+\tau$ of shortfall. So only a fraction $u_F/(u_F+\tau)$ can fall below the cut when $u_F>0$. The filtration keeps the rest of the rank. Its images under the period maps then give the target rank estimate used in the integral proof of the slope bound.

rows.name: Formalism.L2.Th1.CM.ltLog
rows.plain: The height-two Lubin–Tate logarithm
rows.note: The height-two logarithm has a term of degree $\ell^{2j}$ with coefficient $\ell^{-j}$ for each $j\ge 0$. At an inert prime it relates the integral parameter of the CM formal group to the coordinate used for differentiation.
rows.annotation: The first nonlinear coefficient is $1/\ell$, at degree $\ell^2$. Choose $\varpi$ with $\varpi^{\ell^2-1}=\ell$; the coefficient of $X^{\ell^{2j}}$ in $\varpi^{-1}\log_F(\varpi X)$ has valuation $1+\ell^2+\cdots+\ell^{2(j-1)}-j\ge0$ for $j\ge1$. This series has linear coefficient one, so its inverse is integral. Undoing the rescaling gives the loss of at most $(r-1)/(\ell^2-1)$ in degree $r$; the first nonlinear coefficient of the inverse is $-1/\ell$, so the bound is sharp in that degree.

rows.plain: Coefficient bounds for the inverse Lubin–Tate logarithm
rows.note: Inverting the logarithm can cost at most $(r-1)/(\ell^2-1)$ in valuation in degree $r$. Passing from a Taylor coefficient to a derivative supplies the valuation of $r!$, giving the rate $\ell/(\ell^2-1)$ per order up to logarithmic loss.
rows.annotation: Let $\mathsf g$ be the inverse of $\upsilon\log_F$. For $r\ge1$, a product contributing to $[z^r]\mathsf g(z)^k$ has $k$ positive degrees adding to $r$, hence valuation at least $-\rho_\ell(r-k)$. Thus the coefficient of an integral series $\vartheta(\mathsf g(z))$ loses at most $\rho_\ell(r-1)$, while its derivative gains $v_\ell(r!)=r/(\ell-1)-s_\ell(r)/(\ell-1)$, where $s_\ell(r)$ is the base-$\ell$ digit sum. rows.note: In the polynomial model, belonging to either integral Weyl lattice is equivalent to pairing integrally with every vector of the other lattice, within the given representation. This gives the integral pairings needed in the finite sum for a period.
rows.annotation: Write $\Delta$ and $\nabla$ for the two integral Weyl forms in the weight space. The assertion is that the integrality test against every vector of $\Delta$ characterises membership in $\nabla$, and the reverse test characterises membership in $\Delta$. Merely proving that the pairings of their integral vectors are integral would give inclusions in the dual lattices, rather than equality. After transport to the lattices at the genus classes, this supplies integral numerators in the class sum for the period; it does not clear the denominators from stabiliser orders.

ties.name: minkowski_bound_rat
ties.plain: Minkowski’s order bound for finite rational matrix groups

rows.name: minkowski_bound_rat
rows.plain: Minkowski’s order bound for finite rational matrix groups
rows.note: The finite class sums involve denominators from the orders of stabilisers. Minkowski’s theorem controls these uniformly because the order of every finite subgroup of $\operatorname{GL}_N(\mathbb Q)$ divides the same explicit integer depending only on $N$.
rows.annotation: Write a period as $\sum_c y_c/|\Gamma_c|$, with $y_c$ integral and $\Gamma_c$ the class stabiliser. A finite subgroup of $\mathrm{GL}_N(\mathbb Q)$ preserves the lattice $\sum_{g\in\Gamma_c}g\mathbb Z^N$, so it may be conjugated into $\mathrm{GL}_N(\mathbb Z)$ in the same dimension. Minkowski gives a common multiple, $M_N=\prod_{p\le N+1}p^{\sum_{j\ge0}\lfloor N/(p^j(p-1))\rfloor}$, of the stabiliser orders. Their least common multiple $D_\Gamma$ divides $M_N$; multiplying the period by $D_\Gamma$ makes every summand integral, so its valuation is at least $-v_\lambda(D_\Gamma)$, independently of the number of classes.

rows.note: For each period map, the diagonal Gram block measures how far the weighted map is from an isometry. The other two tests bound the overlap of distinct maps on the scale $d_i d_j/D^*$ and cap the common target dimension at $(1+\eta_1)D^*$.
rows.annotation: Put $R=\sum_i d_i$, $D=|\alpha|$ and $Q=\sum_i\gamma_i B_iB_i^*$. Then $\operatorname{tr}Q\ge(1-\sqrt{e_0})R$ and, by cyclicity of trace, $\operatorname{tr}(Q^2)=\sum_{i,j}\|\Gamma_{ij}\|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2\le (1+\eta_0)R^2/D^*+(1+\sqrt{e_0})^2R$. The excess of this ratio over one measures the relative variance of the eigenvalues of $Q$; it is the abundance of words ($D^*/R$ small) that makes the diagonal contribution to it small. rows.note: The two Poincaré series are paired by summing operators indexed by integral double cosets. The sum gives a single operator on the spaces of coefficient vectors, so each contribution to the Gram bounds can be estimated before reassembling the pairing.
rows.annotation: On the spaces of values at class representatives, the operator $K$ is the normalised $\mathcal P_u^*\mathcal P_{u'}$, from the $u'$-space to the $u$-space. The block for a pair of class representatives in a double-coset term is zero unless the finite representative meets the level condition; otherwise it is a scalar times the integral of the rank-one operators $W_u(x)W_{u'}(g_\infty^{-1}x)^*$, with $g_\infty$ the infinite component of the representative. Relevance is a separate condition, the agreement of the unipotent characters on the common subgroup; the irrelevant terms vanish by `LemmaV`. Thus the expansion is of the Gram operator itself, not of its norm: one can remove terms by vanishing before estimating the remainder.

rows.plain: The identity term acts by a scalar
rows.note: The diagonal orbital integral for a unipotent representative is a scalar times the identity on the representation before normalization. Its scalar is a conjugated character value times the product of the two volumes divided by the representation dimension.
rows.annotation: For a diagonal term with representative in $\mathbf N$, covariance takes the factor $\overline{\psi(g_\infty^{-1})}$ out of the integral. The integral left over is that of $W_u(x)W_u(x)^*$; it commutes with the compact group at infinity and hence is scalar by irreducibility of $\pi_u$. Its trace, by the quotient norm-one condition on $W_u$ and the measure decomposition, is $\mathrm{vol}(\mathbf N\text{-domain})\mathrm{vol}(\mathbf H)$, so division by $\dim\pi_u$ gives the scalar. For each class the unique contributing identity coset has its character phase cancelled by the finite-level character and its volume factors cancelled by the normalisation (including the level volume); summing these terms gives the identity on the space of forms, not just on the weight space.

rows.note: An off-diagonal orbital integral for a relevant degenerate coset must intertwine the two representations on the coset’s pointwise stabilizer. When their archimedean parameters differ at every place, the intertwining condition forces the operator to be zero.
rows.annotation: For a relevant degenerate coset, the pointwise stabiliser of the sum of the two isotropic subspaces supplies the actions of a product of groups $\mathrm U(k)$, one at each infinite place, conjugated on the second space. This removes the degenerate terms exactly off the diagonal, whereas on the diagonal their norms have to be estimated.

rows.annotation: Here the gap is in the parameters of the single discrete series on $\mathbf G$, not the separation between words in the preceding item. rows.name: Formalism.MainNotions.BesselId
rows.plain: Bessel pairings agree up to isometries and a nonzero scalar
rows.note: The same isometry of the common target works for every Bessel pairing, with a source isometry and a nonzero scalar allowed to depend on the word. The definition also requires that the abstract maps restrict to the given pairings over the coefficient field.
rows.annotation: The map $B_u$ of [Section 5.2](pdf#subsection.5.2) pairs a form with the test-vector space; `BesselId` identifies this pairing with that of $\mathcal P_u$ against the same embedded space inside the larger space of forms. The target isometry is common to all words: in a cross Gram block the two source isometries act on opposite sides and the common target isometry cancels, while the nonzero scalar of a word can be absorbed by changing its positive weight by the reciprocal of its squared modulus. Independent target isometries would not in general preserve the cross Gram blocks. The extensions for the slope theorem are the full Poincaré-series maps restricted to the ramified sources, not their compressions to the test-vector space; a separate dimension bound controls the extra target directions.

rows.name: UpperTheory.Top.VVle
rows.plain: Bound the log-weighted sum of twisted cohomology lengths
rows.fidelity_note: `VVle E t B` fixes the host field, twist cutoff and upper bound. For each choice of algebraic closure and local data it first requires finite Sha length for every prime and $1\le e<t$, then bounds the sum over each finite set of primes by $B$. The summands are nonnegative, so the supremum of the finite sums is the full sum in the paper. The scale-dependent choices of $t$ and $B$ and the window quantifiers belong to `VAt` and `VWin`.
rows.annotation: The length is that over $\mathbb Z_\ell$ of the classes unramified outside the places above $\ell$ and infinity and locally trivial above $\ell$, not of the whole $H^1(G_\Sigma,\mathbb Q_\ell/\mathbb Z_\ell(-e))$. Each composition factor has order $\ell$, so $\log\ell\,\operatorname{len}_\ell(e)=\log|\mathrm{Sha}(E,\ell,e)|$. The inequality bounds the product of the orders by $\exp(\sqrt b)$; in particular at a fixed scale at most $\sqrt b/\log 2$ pairs $(\ell,e)$ in the indicated range can have a nonzero group. The prime $2$ is included.

rows.name: UpperTheory.Top.VWin
rows.plain: Windowed cohomology bounds for every primitive character
rows.note: `VWin` fixes the exponent $401$. For each primitive character, $0<\varepsilon<1/52$ and a function choosing an admissible cyclotomic layer at every $x\ge1$, Lean chooses $J$ and a starting scale $X_0$. For each $X\ge X_0$ and each eligible prime pair at $X^{1/J}$, it then chooses $[Y,Y^2]\subseteq[X^{1/J},X]$. The same pair is used throughout that window, and the bound is required for every matching host field at every scale in it. The paper abbreviates this order of choices.

For that very pair, `VWinAt` gives a square window $[Y_1,Y_1^2]$ inside this interval on which the cohomological bound with cutoff $\lfloor x^{401}\rfloor$ holds at every scale, for every field of the prescribed kind. Thus both estimates hold on the same window, although the layer of the host varies with $x$.

ties.fidelity_note: `VVle E t B` fixes the host field, twist cutoff and upper bound. For each choice of algebraic closure and local data it first requires finite Sha length for every prime and $1\le e<t$, then bounds the sum over each finite set of primes by $B$. The summands are nonnegative, so the supremum of the finite sums is the full sum in the paper. The scale-dependent choices of $t$ and $B$ and the window quantifiers belong to `VAt` and `VWin`.

explanation.text: The group $\operatorname{Sha}(E,\ell,e)$ consists of global cohomology classes that become trivial at each place above $\ell$, with coefficients twisted by the $-e$ power of the cyclotomic character. The length of a finite such group is the base-$\ell$ logarithm of its order. Multiplying by $\log\ell$ and summing therefore controls the total logarithmic size across primes and twists. The twists come from differences between the cyclotomic powers in the Galois representations of the lifts. Their total contributes to an upper bound for the logarithmic index of a sublattice at each lift level. The slope argument uses this bound to control the loss from passing to the sublattice. The lattice index estimate allows an error of size $b$. The contribution from the cohomological bound is only of order $\sqrt b$. The window supplies this control at every scale of an interval, as required for the later zero-free argument.

rows.note: The product map evaluates at the eigensystems outside the lift subset. Its kernel is the ideal.
rows.fidelity_note: `ccIdeal` takes the kernel of the simultaneous evaluations outside the supplied finite set $Z$. The record's `cc` applies it to the full lift set.
rows.annotation: Over the fraction field of $\mathcal O$ one can separate the eigensystems by idempotents. Over $\mathcal O$ one may not be able to: for example, with $\mathfrak m$ the maximal ideal and $s\ge1$, take $\mathbf T=\{(a,b)\in\mathcal O^2:a\equiv b\pmod{\mathfrak m^s}\}$ and let $\mathcal Z$ consist of the first eigensystem. The kernel in question is $\mathfrak m^s\times\{0\}$. Its values on the first eigensystem form the ideal $\mathfrak m^s$, of valuation $s/e_{\mathcal O}$, with ramification index $e_{\mathcal O}$, in the normalisation $v_\ell(\ell)=1$. In general `ccAt` is this ideal of values at a single lift $\pi$; a congruence with an eigensystem outside $\mathcal Z$ makes every integral operator vanishing outside $\mathcal Z$ small at $\pi$.

rows.name: Formalism.BasicNotions.NData.etaLoc
rows.plain: Local length of the congruence module
rows.note: The local length is the length of the quotient of MtUp by MtLow.
rows.fidelity_note: `etaLoc` forms the two lattices using $Z_{\mathrm{good}}$ and its complement. The printed quotient uses $Z$ and its complement. Lean normalizes the length of the quotient by $\operatorname{length}_{\mathcal O}(\mathcal O/\ell\mathcal O)$.
rows.annotation: If $p_{\mathcal Z}$ denotes projection onto $V_{\mathcal Z}$ along the complementary eigenspaces, the numerator of the displayed quotient is $p_{\mathcal Z}(\mathcal M)$ and the denominator is $\mathcal M\cap V_{\mathcal Z}$. An integral Hecke operator $f$ in the congruence ideal satisfies $f p_{\mathcal Z}(v)=fv\in\mathcal M\cap V_{\mathcal Z}$ for $v\in\mathcal M$: it annihilates the quotient. The actual `etaLoc` takes the quotient for the good lifts $\mathcal Z_{\rm good}\subseteq\mathcal Z$, with length divided by $\operatorname{len}_{\mathcal O}(\mathcal O/\ell\mathcal O)$; separating them from the other lifts costs an additional factor $|G|$ from the finite level group. The resulting bound is $\eta_{\rm loc}\le\sum_{\pi\in\mathcal Z_{\rm good}}\dim V_\pi\bigl(v_\ell(I_\pi)+v_\ell(|G|)\bigr)$, where $\dim V_\pi$ is the dimension over the fraction field and $I_\pi$ is the congruence ideal evaluated at $\pi$ for the original subset $\mathcal Z$.

explanation.text: Think of a Hecke operator as a function of its eigenvalues. Requiring it to vanish off $Z$ gives an integral way to isolate the lift eigensystems. On the lattice side, project an integral vector to the lift eigenspaces using the fraction-field decomposition. Its projection can fail to belong to the integral lattice there, even though the original vector was integral. The quotient measures this failure for the chosen set of eigensystems.

rows.annotation: The construction starts with the character $\chi_1$ at $\pi$; off $\mathcal Z$ the representations twisted by $\chi_1^{-1}$ have no invariant vector. A determinant estimate bounds the valuation of the congruence ideal by the lengths of cocycle modules with coefficients in the constituents after this twist: $\rho\otimes\chi_1^{-1}$ for the Selmer term, and $\chi_c\chi_1^{-1}=\chi_{\rm cyc}^{-(c-1)}$ for the character terms. Removing ramification at $\mathcal Q$ costs the last term of the statement, once per character. The local hypotheses make the cocycles for $c>1$ unramified away from $\ell$ and coboundaries above $\ell$, so their $\mathbb Z_\ell$-coordinates give classes in $\mathrm{Sha}(E,\ell,c-1)$; for $c=1$ the coefficients are untwisted and the everywhere unramified classes are bounded by the class number.

rows.name: UpperTheory.V.HV.Core.of_four_alt
rows.plain: Assemble windowed cohomology bounds by cases
rows.note: `of_four_alt` takes the literature record, `LemmaK`, and `CountI`, `CountII`, `CountIII`, `CountV`. The proof supplies the `ThmBab` input using Ferrero–Washington, converts `ML.iv` to the required odd bound, and supplies `CountZ` before calling `vwin_of_counts`. The conclusion is VWin. Its proof combines four count bounds with the even and odd cohomological inputs.
rows.annotation: At an odd prime $\ell$, split the length into the parts of signs $(-1)^{e+1}$ and $(-1)^e$ under complex conjugation; the prime $2$ is treated separately. On the latter side, for fixed $e$, every case other than Case I has $\ell$ in a fixed finite set $B_\chi$ (depending on the character defining the host) or $\ell-1\mid 2e$, hence in the second instance $\ell\le2e+1$. Thus `CountI` has to bound the sum over arbitrary finite sets of coefficient primes, whereas the other counts can be summed over a bounded range of primes or supplied by the tower estimates at the fixed primes. If $B_2,B_-,B_+$ bound the sum of lengths at $2$ and the logarithmically weighted sums at odd primes of signs $(-1)^{e+1}$ and $(-1)^e$, respectively, the left side of [Statement 8.1](pdf#theorem.8.1) is at most $B_2\log2+B_-+B_+$; on the common window the bounds for these three quantities are $\exp(x^{4\varepsilon/5})$, $O(\exp(8x^{\varepsilon/4}))$ and $O(\exp(x^{4\varepsilon/5})+(\operatorname{cond}E\,t_0)^C)$. Since $\log(\operatorname{cond}E\,t_0)\le2x^{\varepsilon/4}$, their sum is eventually less than $\exp(x^\varepsilon/2)=\sqrt b$.

explanation.text: Each count controls a class of primes and twists in the total length. The bounds need to hold at the same scales before they can be added. The assembly proof first obtains simultaneous windows for the inputs whose estimates depend on the scale, then incorporates the separate parity estimate. Ferrero–Washington supplies the vanishing of $\mu$ for the cyclotomic-tower input. The crude finiteness bound covers twists outside that input's range.

ties.name: UpperTheory.V.Odd.PsiBound
ties.plain: Bound odd cohomology by a special-value valuation

rows.name: UpperTheory.V.Odd.PsiBound
rows.plain: Bound odd cohomology by a special-value valuation
rows.note: When $\ell$ is odd and does not divide the field degree, the Sha eigenspace with complex-conjugation sign $(-1)^{e+1}$ has length bounded by the valuation of a scaled Bernoulli value. The sign reverses when the twist $e$ increases by one.
rows.annotation: Let $\chi$ be the character modulo $N$ obtained by pulling back $\psi$ along the cyclotomic action, and $\chi^*$ its primitive inducing character, of conductor $f$. In `PsiBound` the explicit value is $a=\operatorname{den}(N,e+1)B_{e+1,\chi^*}$, where $B_{e+1,\chi^*}=f^e\sum_{r=1}^{f}\chi^*(r)B_{e+1}(r/f)$ and $\operatorname{den}(N,e+1)$ clears denominators. For odd $\ell\nmid[E:\mathbb Q]$, with $\psi$ valued in the units of a discrete valuation ring $\mathcal O$ finite over $\mathbb Z_\ell$ and $a\in\mathcal O$, the assertion for $e\ge1$ and $\chi(-1)=(-1)^{e+1}$ is $\operatorname{len}_{\mathcal O}(\mathrm{Sha}(E,\ell,e)_\psi)\le v_{\mathcal O}(a)$. Thus a unit special value gives a zero eigenspace; a nonzero value of positive valuation gives a finite bound for its length, not necessarily zero.

ties.name: UpperTheory.V.ML.iv
ties.plain: The odd cohomology bound from Poitou–Tate duality

rows.name: UpperTheory.V.ML.iv
rows.plain: The odd cohomology bound from Poitou–Tate duality
rows.note: `ML.iv` takes Poitou–Tate duality and unramified orthogonality and concludes `PsiBound`. Unfolded, the bound applies to abelian CM fields with the indicated cyclotomic action and $\ell\ne2$, $\ell\nmid[E:\mathbb Q]$. The character must have sign $(-1)^{e+1}$ at complex conjugation.
rows.annotation: The call `recip h₁ h₂` supplies the reciprocity input to `psiOf`, which gives the preceding character bound. When $\ell$ is prime to $[E:\mathbb Q]$, the character projectors are integral over a coefficient ring containing the character values, so the eigenspace bounds can be added after normalising lengths. The point of bounding algebraic special values is that, for a nonzero algebraic integer, the sum of its local integral valuations with the weights $f_w\log\ell$ at places $w\mid\ell$ ($f_w$ the residue degree) is the logarithm of the absolute norm. The associated `PrimeBound` states a bound of this form: $\sum_{\ell\in S}\log\ell\,\operatorname{len}_\ell^-(e)\le [E:\mathbb Q]\log(\operatorname{bnd}(N,e+1))$ for every finite set $S$ of odd primes prime to the degree, with finiteness separately asserted. The input actually passed to `of_four_alt` is the broader odd-part estimate obtained by `Odd.thmBcFree_of`.

explanation.text: Look at one Galois character at a time. When its sign has the required parity, the argument bounds the cohomology length by the valuation of a generalized Bernoulli number multiplied by a denominator-clearing factor. The Kolyvagin derivative step relates the restriction of the next class to inertia at an auxiliary prime to the previous class evaluated at Frobenius there. Poitou–Tate duality and the orthogonality of unramified classes are the local-to-global inputs to the bound.
