ties.name: UpperTheory.V.ML.kolStep
ties.plain: Kolyvagin’s recursion at an auxiliary prime

rows.name: UpperTheory.V.ML.kolStep
rows.plain: Kolyvagin’s recursion at an auxiliary prime
rows.note: Add a new auxiliary prime $q$ to the list used to form the Kolyvagin derivative. Under the admissibility conditions, the new class on the specified inertia element at $q$ is a stated multiple of the old class on Frobenius at $q$.
rows.annotation: Let $n$ be the product of the old auxiliary primes and let $q$ be a new admissible prime. Write $y=D_Lx(n)$ and $w=D_Lx(qn)$ for the elements after applying the old derivatives: the Euler-system relations give $N_qw=(y/\phi^{-1}y)^{s(n,q)}$ and $w\equiv(\phi^{-1}y)^{s(n,q)}$ at a place above $q$, where $\phi$ is Frobenius there. Applying the derivative at $q$ and these two relations shows that the roots of unity $\zeta^{\kappa'(t)}$ and $\zeta^{s(n,q)\kappa(\phi^{-1})}$ have equal reductions; since $q\nmid M$ and $\zeta$ has order $M$, they are equal. The old homomorphism has $\kappa(\phi^{-1})=-\kappa(\phi)$, giving $\kappa'(t)=-s(n,q)\kappa(\phi)$: an evaluation of the old class at Frobenius is read as an evaluation of the new one at the prescribed inertia element $t$.

ties.name: UpperTheory.V.FW.sinnott
ties.plain: Sinnott’s vanishing lemma for coefficients

rows.name: UpperTheory.V.FW.sinnott
rows.plain: Sinnott’s vanishing lemma for coefficients
rows.note: Sinnott’s step works modulo a sufficiently high power of $\ell$. If the difference of a function and its translate is supported on a fixed interval, and the sum of the function’s rescalings by the specified $\ell$-adic units vanishes, the coefficients on that interval all vanish under the stated independence condition.
rows.annotation: Suppose $\alpha(y)-\alpha(y-N)=\sum_{s<N,\,s\equiv y\pmod{\ell^n}}P(s)$ on $\mathbb Z/\ell^n\mathbb Z$ and $\sum_i\alpha(\eta_i^{-1}y)=0$, where the units $\eta_i$ in $\mathbb Z_\ell$ have no common nonzero integer multiples in pairs. Write $P_i=\sum_{s<N}P(s)[s\eta_i]$ in the group algebra, with $[u][v]=[u+v]$. Applying the product of the difference operators gives the reduction of $\sum_i P_i\prod_{j\ne i}(1-[N\eta_j])=0$ modulo $\ell^n$; the support before reduction is fixed independently of $P$, so for large $n$ the identity holds in the group algebra of $\mathbb Z_\ell$ itself. In the additive quotient by the subgroup $\mathbb Z N\eta_i$, all terms but the $i$-th vanish. Each remaining factor $1-[N\eta_j]$ acts injectively on finitely supported elements, since $N\eta_j$ has infinite order in the quotient by the independence assumption. Hence $P_i=0$ there, and its $N$ distinct basis elements give $P(s)=0$ for $s<N$.

ties.name: UpperTheory.V.LemmaK
ties.plain: A uniform bound on twisted second cohomology

rows.name: UpperTheory.V.LemmaK
rows.plain: A uniform bound on twisted second cohomology
rows.note: For the twists outside the cyclotomic-tower estimate, the paper uses a bound on the logarithm of the order of the degree-two cohomology group. Its inputs are the twist, the degree and the absolute discriminant of a totally complex field containing the required roots of unity, including a primitive fourth root when $\ell=2$.
rows.annotation: For a totally complex field $F$ of degree $n$ and absolute discriminant $D$, `LemmaK` gives finiteness of $H^2(G_\Sigma,\mathbb Z_\ell(e+1))$ and $\log\#H^2\le\exp((2en)^{C_K}\log(2D))$; it requires $\mu_\ell\subset F$ at odd $\ell$ and $\mu_4\subset F$ at $2$. The tower estimate leaves a bounded number of exceptional positive integers $e$ for which this crude bound is needed at the base of the tower. For any one of them the forbidden scales are those with $e\le x^{401}$ but $e>x^{\varepsilon/(2C_K)}$, an interval $[e^{1/401},e^{2C_K/\varepsilon})$ when nonempty. On taking logarithms each such interval has a bounded ratio of endpoints, so a bounded number of them can be avoided by a square window inside $[X^{1/J},X]$ for large enough fixed $J$. On that window every exceptional twist in range is small enough for the base-field estimate; no twist in the required range is discarded.

ties.name: UpperTheory.V.Z.J.NumberU3U_s
ties.plain: A congruence integer for definite rank-three unitary groups

rows.name: UpperTheory.V.Z.J.NumberU3U_s
rows.plain: A congruence integer for definite rank-three unitary groups
rows.note: One nonzero integer is chosen before the coefficient prime $\ell$. At each $\ell\ne 2,p$, the sum of valuations of the nonzero differences between the admissible representations’ traces and the Eisenstein trace is at most the valuation of that integer, so the sum weighted by $\log\ell$ is at most its logarithmic size.
rows.annotation: Put $q=\mathrm N\lambda$. The finite trace list $(t_s)$ counts the rank-three cuspidal eigensystems and the rank-two newforms with a trivial summand adjoined, not merely their distinct numerical trace values. The product of $q^e(t_s-\mathrm{eis}(z_o))$ over $s,o$ is an integer because its factors are algebraic integers permuted by Galois, and is nonzero since the trace bound $|t_s|\le\sqrt q+2$ is less than $q^e-1-q^{-e}\le|\mathrm{eis}(z_o)|$ for $q\ge7$. Each factor has log absolute value at most $2e\log q+1$, and the cohomological dimension estimate bounds the number of indices by a polynomial in $N(e+1)$. At any coefficient prime $\ell\ne2,p$, the pairwise non-isomorphic admissible representations in each $X_o$ are assigned distinct indices (even when their traces coincide); $q^e$ is an $\ell$-adic unit and all unused factors are integral. Dropping those factors can only increase the absolute value of the product at $\ell$, giving the stated inequality.

ties.name: UpperTheory.V.Z.J.OneCharU_s
ties.plain: Bound cohomology by valuations of Frobenius trace differences

rows.name: UpperTheory.V.Z.J.OneCharU_s
rows.plain: Bound cohomology by valuations of Frobenius trace differences
rows.note: Fix a character and a Galois element at which no admissible representation has the Eisenstein trace. The corresponding Sha length is finite and is bounded by twice the sum of the trace-difference valuations over a finite set of pairwise nonisomorphic admissible representations.
rows.annotation: For a character $\psi$ in an orbit satisfying the hypotheses of Case I, write $L_\psi$ for its coefficient-ring length and $v_\ell$ for the valuation with $v_\ell(\ell)=1$. Use the preceding integer statement with a singleton (for each admissible representation) to obtain the trace non-equality at $\mathrm{Fr}_\lambda^{-1}$ required by `OneCharU_s`; the latter then gives finiteness and a bound for $V_n(\psi)=L_\psi/\operatorname{len}_{\mathcal O}(\mathcal O/\ell\mathcal O)$ by twice the sum of the trace-difference valuations in its finite family. Applying the integer statement to all these families at once and taking additive valuations gives $\sum_\psi V_n(\psi)\le2v_\ell(NN)$, so the sum weighted by $\log\ell$ costs at most $2\log|NN|$ for $\ell\ne2,p$; a second test prime covers $p$, and $2$ is treated separately. These Eisenstein congruences bound the character pieces of Sha; in [Statement 8.2](pdf#theorem.8.2) the lengths of Sha in turn bound the congruences between theta lifts and other eigensystems.

ties.name: UpperTheory.V.Alg.LemmaM
ties.plain: Bound cotangent length by valuations at covering points

rows.name: UpperTheory.V.Alg.LemmaM
rows.plain: Bound cotangent length by valuations at covering points
rows.note: The length to bound is the weight $-1$ part of the cotangent space at the augmentation of a graded algebra. Under the five hypotheses, evaluating one element at a finite set of points that covers the specified ideal gives an upper bound of twice the sum of the resulting valuations.
rows.annotation: In the deformation problem of $r_0=\Psi\oplus1\oplus\Psi^{-1}$, conjugation by $\operatorname{diag}(u,1,u^{-1})$ grades the extension directions; the Selmer length is bounded by the length of the weight $-1$ cotangent module at the base point, modulo the equations of that weight. Set $a=\operatorname{tr}r(\sigma)-\operatorname{tr}r_0(\sigma)$ for the universal representation $r$: it has weight zero, vanishes at the base, and must be nonzero at each point that is neither upper nor lower triangular. The finiteness of the weight-zero algebra as an $\mathcal O$-module modulo the equations (`M2`) and the condition that there is at most one tangent direction at such a point (`M4`, the direction of the grading action) are part of the hypotheses of `LemmaM`. The conclusion is that finitely many orbits cover these points and the cotangent module has finite length, at most $2\sum_{\xi\in T}v(\xi(a))$ for any finite covering set $T$. Thus it is the integral size of the cotangent module at the base, not the dimension of the tangent space over the fraction field, that the trace differences bound.

ties.name: UpperTheory.V.Hi.hida_unitary_of_printed_hida
ties.plain: Unitary Hida families from the printed Hida hypotheses

rows.name: UpperTheory.V.Hi.hida_unitary_of_printed_hida
rows.plain: Unitary Hida families from the printed Hida hypotheses
rows.note: Under the cited Hida hypotheses, the proof constructs an ideal of the universal ordinary determinant ring for the unitary group. The resulting quotient has dense arithmetic points satisfying the required purity and classicality conditions, and the construction supplies automorphy.
rows.annotation: The points whose traces enter the cotangent estimate are initially points of a Galois deformation problem; the trace list above, by contrast, is indexed by automorphic eigensystems. `hida_unitary_of_printed_hida` constructs an ideal $J$ of the ordinary determinant ring $B$ from unitary Hecke data; the ensuing `ModUAlt` gives $B/J$ finite over the weight algebra $\Lambda$, with the density and arithmetic-point properties. The argument propagates automorphy from seed points given by adjoint lifts of ordinary two-dimensional forms congruent to Eisenstein series. It is the later statement on the deformation problem that supplies finiteness and automorphy at the irreducible points and modularity of the two-dimensional pieces at the endoscopic points; the Hida statement alone is not an assertion of automorphy of every point.

ties.name: UpperTheory.V.Z.Kato.Final.zetaUr
ties.plain: Kato’s unramified zeta classes

rows.name: UpperTheory.V.Z.Kato.Final.zetaUr
rows.plain: Kato’s unramified zeta classes
rows.note: For the specified ordinary newform and attached two-dimensional representation, the Kato argument supplies an integral cocycle unramified away from $\ell$. At $\ell$ its projection to the ordinary quotient is nontrivial in cohomology, and at suitable auxiliary primes it has lifts satisfying the stated Frobenius congruence.
rows.annotation: For a representation attached to an $\ell$-ordinary newform of level prime to $\ell$, `zetaUr` supplies an integral class unramified away from $\ell$, lying outside the ordinary local condition at $\ell$, together with derivative data at auxiliary primes. At an eligible endoscopic point $W\oplus1$ the two off-diagonal pieces of the endomorphism representation are $W$ and $W^\vee\simeq W\otimes\theta$, since $\det W=\theta$ is quadratic. The consequence used here (`KatoTwoW`) is the vanishing of the Bloch–Kato Selmer groups for these two pieces, used with the other rigidity hypotheses to rule out extra tangent directions at the point. This is not the Euler-system estimate for the odd part above: here the numerical bound comes from the trace differences, and the Euler system supplies a condition for that bound.

ties.name: UpperTheory.Gal.Int.galoisRepresentations_of_thetaLift
ties.plain: Galois representations for unitary forms from theta lifts

rows.name: UpperTheory.Gal.Int.galoisRepresentations_of_thetaLift
rows.plain: Galois representations for unitary forms from theta lifts
rows.note: Assuming the definite theta-lift theorem, this step attaches a continuous semisimple $\ell$-adic Galois representation to a regular algebraic, polarized cuspidal representation over a CM field. The archimedean type of the cuspidal representation prescribes the Hodge–Tate weights.
rows.annotation:
The geometric step starts in odd rank, with the cohomology of compact Shimura varieties: the Hecke–Frobenius relation constrains the Frobenius eigenvalues, and the genericity and weight-gap conditions serve to cut out a representation of the required dimension. Congruences and limits of traces remove the extra conditions on the forms of odd rank. For even rank $
u$, two lifts to odd rank $
u+t$ have at split unramified places the same twist of the original Satake parameter and two disjoint sets of added global characters $\{\psi_{1i}\}$ and $\{\psi_{2i}\}$. Writing $r_j$ for the Galois representation of the $j$-th lift and $\psi_{ji}$ also for its added $\ell$-adic characters, comparison at the split places identifies the two virtual representations $[r_j]-\sum_i[\psi_{ji}]$ ($j=1,2$); a negative multiplicity in their common value would require a character in both added sets, so this value is an actual semisimple representation. Undoing the twist, and using descent of the automorphic forms and patching over quadratic CM extensions, gives the assertion for $\mathrm{GL}_
u$; in [Statement 8.2](pdf#theorem.8.2) it is the eigensystems off the lift subset as well as those in it that need Galois representations.

ties.name: UpperTheory.GalStar.AwayB
ties.plain: Partial local compatibility away from the coefficient prime

rows.name: UpperTheory.GalStar.AwayB
rows.plain: Partial local compatibility away from the coefficient prime
rows.note: The Galois and automorphic Weil–Deligne parameters have the same dimension at places away from $\ell$. A split character parameter with zero monodromy gives equality, while the stated tame square-free case over $\mathbb Q_p$ with zero monodromy gives agreement of the characteristic polynomials on inertia.
rows.annotation: At the split unramified places used in the congruence argument the equality given by `tor` supplies the Frobenius polynomials in `GoodR`. At the two auxiliary level primes, totally split and with $p>16\nu^2$, the condition called square-free permits a repeated eigenvalue of the tame generator if it is a $(p-1)$-st root of unity; in particular it permits the repeated eigenvalue of the character block. The clause `tame0` gives agreement of the inertia polynomials and also zero monodromy, without which a unipotent part of the inertia action could escape the polynomial comparison. In the application one obtains a polynomial $P$ over the Hecke algebra with $P_y(r_y(\gamma_0))(r_y(\gamma)-\chi_1(\gamma))=0$ at the eigensystems $y$, for inertia elements $\gamma$ and a tame generator $\gamma_0$; here $P_y$ is the specialisation at $y$, and $P_\pi(\chi_1(\gamma_0))$ is required to be a unit at the lift $\pi$. This is the relation used to make the relevant congruence cocycles unramified; equality of Frobenius actions at these ramified places is not needed.

ties.name: UpperTheory.TP.TLiftK
ties.plain: Theta lifting between definite unitary groups

rows.name: UpperTheory.TP.TLiftK
rows.plain: Theta lifting between definite unitary groups
rows.note: The theta-lift hypothesis concerns pairs of definite unitary groups, with Hermitian source and skew-Hermitian target. Once the target rank is large enough, the lift is supplied for source representations satisfying the required weight inequality at each infinite place.
rows.annotation: The threshold $n_0$ is chosen for the fixed good base datum and the source of rank $n_1$, with Hermitian matrix $1$; it precedes the choice of the target (of skew-Hermitian matrix $\delta\,1$), the form and the two splitting characters. At an infinite place $w$ of the real subfield, write $m_X(w),m_W(w)$ for the exponents of these characters. In the range $n_2\ge n_1$ the weight of the lift has $n_2-n_1$ entries equal to $(n_1+m_X(w))/2$; the other $n_1$ entries are this number plus $\lambda_{w,k}-(n_2+m_W(w))/2$, respectively, where $\lambda_w$ is the source weight. The hypothesis $n_2+m_W(w)\le2\lambda_{w,k}$ thus puts the first block at or above the added block. For the passage from even to odd rank one chooses a large odd $n_2$ and a splitting character of the prescribed restriction with $m_W(w)\le2\min_k\lambda_{w,k}-n_2$ at every $w$: it is not necessary to increase the weights of the original form.

ties.name: UpperTheory.TP.K.tLiftK
ties.plain: Construct the definite unitary theta lifts

rows.name: UpperTheory.TP.K.tLiftK
rows.plain: Construct the definite unitary theta lifts
rows.note: The definite theta-lift existence theorem is proved by applying the construction in the theta-kernel files. This is the argument supplied when the Galois-representation theorem asks for the lift as a hypothesis.
rows.annotation: For a non-zero form $\phi$ and Schwartz datum $f$, the theta lift is $\int\theta_f(g,h)\overline{\phi(g)}\,dg$ over the source quotient. Write $c_\phi(g)=\langle R(g)\phi,\phi\rangle$ for the matrix coefficient of right translation and $C_f$ for the Weil coefficient in the Rallis formula: in the range $n_2\ge2n_1$, with $n_2/2$ larger than an integrability exponent of a height on the source group, it suffices to make $\int C_f(g)\overline{c_\phi(g)}\,dg$ non-zero. Schur orthogonality for the compact group at infinity gives a non-zero scalar factor, and the finite-place Schwartz data concentrate the Weil coefficient near the identity, where $c_\phi(1)=\|\phi\|^2>0$; a bound on the tail prevents cancellation. From the non-zero lift one takes an irreducible constituent, with the stated weights and the local theta pairings at split places. No non-vanishing of a special value of an $L$-function has to be established separately for this construction.

rows.name: UpperTheory.Top.IsChiField
rows.plain: The cyclotomic fixed-field condition for a host
rows.note: Read the four conditions on $r$ as a membership test for the subgroup fixing the host inside the cyclotomic field. The two quadratic-residue conditions specify the contributions of the auxiliary primes $q$ and $d$ to the field.
rows.annotation: Let $E_0$ be the compositum of the real cyclotomic layer $\mathbb Q(\zeta_{2^{e_2+2}})^+$ and the field cut out by $\psi$ (the fixed field of its kernel in the cyclotomic field of its conductor). The first two tests say that the automorphism fixes $E_0$; the last two say that it fixes $\sqrt{-q}$ and $\sqrt{-d}$. Thus $E=E_0(\sqrt{-q},\sqrt{-d})$. The first two fields may intersect, but the two quadratic fields have distinct new prime conductors, prime to the conductor of $E_0$; consequently each contributes a separate sign to the Galois group, and every character of $E$ is a character of $E_0$ times a choice of the two quadratic characters.

rows.plain: Mean-square estimate over prime moduli
rows.note: `meanSqK` bounds the sum of squares over candidate primes in the admissible progression for every $y\in[Y,Y^K]$, with the stated restrictions on prime divisors of the progression modulus. `stage` uses this bound to control how many candidates exceed the threshold anywhere in the window. This is the mean-square statement on a power window under the stated conditions on the moduli.
rows.annotation: Put $Z=Y^{400A}$ and $S_p(y)=\sum_{n\le Z}\Lambda(n)\min(1,y/n)\kappa(n)(\frac np)$, where $\kappa$ is fixed and $|\kappa|\le1$. The weight comes from [(4.1)](pdf#equation.4.1): replacing $L'/L(1,\chi)$ by its truncated negative prime sum leaves $-1$ for $n\le y$ and $-y/n$ for $y<n\le Z$, so $G_\chi(y)=-S_p(y)$ up to the logarithmic-derivative tail. On expanding $|S_p(y)|^2$, the character factor at $n,m$ is $(\frac{nm}{p})$; after removing square factors and the factors fixed by the progression, quadratic reciprocity reduces the nonconstant averages to sums of $(\frac ps)$ with odd squarefree $s\le Z^2$. The proof uses `twistK` to bound these except for one possible exceptional modulus, and bounds the remaining contributions separately, obtaining mean square $\le Cy\log y$. At a fixed $y$ the share with $|S_p(y)|>\tfrac12 y^{1/2+\varepsilon/2}$ is therefore at most $4Cy^{-\varepsilon}\log y$; a separate maximum estimate is needed to select one prime good for the whole window.

rows.note: `zero_density_box` bounds by $CQ^{1/4}$ the number of primitive characters of modulus at most $Q$ with at least one zero in $\operatorname{Re}s>1-1/400$, $|\operatorname{Im}s|\le Q$, for $Q\ge3$. rows.annotation: The zero-density estimate counts primitive characters having at least one zero in $\operatorname{Re}s>1-1/400$, $|\operatorname{Im}s|\le Q$, with conductor at most $Q$; there are at most $CQ^{1/4}$ such characters. Since there are only finitely many base characters (also with $q$ fixed in the second choice), the box can exclude only $O_{M_0}(U^{1/4+o(1)})$ of the at least $U^{9/10}$ candidates. On the remaining primes the logarithmic-derivative tail is controlled by the zero-free box, and the finite sum by the mean-square estimate.

explanation.text: A prime can fail the bound at a different scale from its neighbours. The proof handles this by controlling the maximum of the smoothed sum on each dyadic interval using the mean square and an integral of the squared derivative. The upper bounds for the counts of bad primes form a geometric series over the dyadic intervals. Zero density controls the separate set whose twists have zeros near $1$. The combined count leaves primes that pass both tests.

rows.plain: Behrend’s set avoids bounded three-point relations
rows.note: Encode the lattice points on a Behrend sphere as integers in a base large enough that a relation with the bounded coefficients would hold digit by digit. Three distinct points on a sphere cannot be collinear, which rules out the relation.
rows.annotation: Take the integer points $v$ of one squared norm in a box $[0,D)^s$, and map $v$ to $\sum_m v_m B^m$ with $B=4LD$. If three images satisfy the forbidden relation, the resulting signed digit at position $m$ is $j(v_{2,m}-v_{1,m})-i(v_{3,m}-v_{1,m})$, of absolute value at most $2L(D-1)<B$. Reduction modulo $B$ makes the first digit zero, and division by $B$ repeats the argument at every subsequent digit. The same relation then holds between the vectors, so three distinct points of the sphere would lie on a line, which is impossible.

rows.plain: Existence of a thick set without short three-point relations
rows.note: The existence theorem adds a size guarantee to the Behrend construction. For an ambient size $n$ and a coefficient bound $L\ge2$, it supplies a set with $4Ls<n$ for every element $s$, no forbidden three-point relations, and at least $(n/L)\exp(-32\sqrt{\log n\,\log L})$ elements.
rows.annotation: Let $N=|A_0|$, with generator $a_0$, and take $T_2$ to consist of the elements $sa_0$ for the integers $s$ supplied by `hostThickExists`. The condition $4Ls<N$ implies that a relation with coefficients $|i|,|j|\le L$ modulo $N$ is already an integer relation. Hence three visits within $L$ consecutive positions of an orbit of order greater than $4L$ are impossible: subtracting the first visit eliminates the translate, and eliminating the step gives the forbidden relation. An orbit of order $r\le4L$ cannot even meet the set in two distinct elements, for then $r(s_2-s_1)$ would be a nonzero multiple of $N$ of absolute value less than $N$. The bound $|T_2|\ge (N/L)\exp(-32\sqrt{\log N\log L})$ loses only a factor $x^{o(1)}$ for $N\asymp_\psi x^{2+8\varepsilon}$ and $L=O(\log x)$, leaving the density $\delta_T\ge x^{-\varepsilon}$ required in [Section 4.4](pdf#subsection.4.4).

rows.annotation: In this version one has data for a CM type and its dual, with a lower bound for the mean of their logarithmic periods. In the proposed bound `OCCMEstimate`, the main error is $(xL/m+xmL/k)/r+x\eta/m+xL/f+kfL^2$, where $L=\log(al)$, $0<r\le1$ and $l=2f+1$; there are separate errors from the period bound and from omitted primes. Even with the logarithms and $1/r$ suppressed, the product of $x/m,\,xm/k,\,x/f,\,kf$ is $x^3$, so the largest of these four costs is at least $x^{3/4}$. Taking $m\asymp x^{1/4}$, $k\asymp x^{1/2}$ and $f\asymp x^{1/4}$ makes all four of that order; the other hypotheses bound the remaining errors at $x^{3/4+O(\varepsilon)}$. Thus it is a change in the error terms, not merely in the choice of $m$, that is needed to obtain the square-root exponent of [Section 4.4](pdf#subsection.4.4).

ties.name: Formalism.LFunctionChainParameters.characterSumData.AskMainBalance
ties.plain: Count balance when ramification is limited to three host primes

rows.name: Formalism.LFunctionChainParameters.characterSumData.AskMainBalance
rows.plain: Count balance when ramification is limited to three host primes
rows.note: This proposition expresses the deviation of a weighted prime-power count from its main term as a sum over characters, for hosts ramified at most at $2$ and two odd primes. Lean proves this form in `colour_balance`. The final theorem uses the version with a finite set of primes in place of $2$ and the first odd prime.
rows.annotation: The earlier formulation of [Statement 4.2](pdf#theorem.4.2) permits ramification only at $2,q_1,d$, where $q_1,d$ are distinct odd primes. At $2,q_1$ both the inertia group and the Frobenius element lie in $\Phi$; hence every Frobenius coset is contained in $\Phi$ and contributes zero to the count over its complement. The same argument applies to any finite set $S$ of primes satisfying these conditions, which is the generalisation in `HostFactsS`. At $d$ the separate term is unchanged; the extra freedom is in the primes at which the host may ramify without contributing to the count.

ties.name: Formalism.LFunctionChainParameters.characterSumData.colour_balance
ties.plain: The count identity with ramification limited to three host primes

rows.name: Formalism.LFunctionChainParameters.characterSumData.colour_balance
rows.plain: The count identity with ramification limited to three host primes
rows.note: Lean expands the weighted prime-power count by character orthogonality and isolates the trivial and quadratic character contributions to the main term. This proof of the balance identity for hosts ramified only among three specified primes is outside the final dependency cone.
rows.annotation: In the proof of `colour_balance` the normalised character sum at a prime power is $2/|I_p|$ on its Frobenius coset, with $I_p$ the inertia group. This gives the weight $2\log p$ at a counted unramified prime power and $\log d$ at the unique element of each coset at $d$ outside $\Phi$. To recover the centred sum, write $W=w(\rho_g)$ and $(a/n-W)_+=W(a/(Wn)-1)_+$; the non-trivial centring correction is then $-a\ell(\psi)$, independent of $W$. Averaging this correction over $g\notin\Phi$ kills all non-trivial characters except $\chi_\Phi$, whose value there is $-1$, leaving $+a\ell(\chi_\Phi)$; the trivial correction gives $a(\log a-1-\gamma-|\Phi|^{-1}\sum_{\rho\in\Phi}\log w(\rho))$ by the partner bijection. These are the terms of $\mathrm{MAIN}$, but the terms $WG_\psi(a/W)$ still depend on the partner and no such cancellation is asserted for them.

ties.name: Formalism.LFunctionChainParameters.ThickSetMeanBounds.GrowthInequalityForm
ties.plain: Prime-sum growth for hosts with restricted ramification

rows.name: Formalism.LFunctionChainParameters.ThickSetMeanBounds.GrowthInequalityForm
rows.plain: Prime-sum growth for hosts with restricted ramification
rows.note: Lean proves an inequality for the smoothed zeta prime sum from the earlier balance identity and bounds on the count and its errors. The compiled RH proof uses the reduction for a weighted family of characters.
rows.annotation: After replacing the thick weights by $b$, average over all of $H$. Only characters trivial on $H$ survive, namely the four characters of $(\mathbb Z/2)^2$; the thick contribution per size and lift is $b\delta_T/2$ times $G+G_\psi-G_{\chi_\Phi}-G_{\chi_\Phi\psi}$ at $a_t/b$, where $\psi$ is the sign of the second factor. The signs are their values on the base class $\sigma$; bounding the three non-trivial sums at $x$ costs $3x^{1/2+\varepsilon}$, and the change of argument costs at most another $x^{1/2+\varepsilon}$. This accounts for the $4x^{1/2+\varepsilon}$ subtracted from $G(x)$ in `GrowthInequalityForm`. In [(4.5)](pdf#equation.4.5), averaging over $A_0\subseteq H$ instead allows characters non-trivial on $H$ to survive; one can retain a prescribed positively weighted family, rather than having to bound every surviving non-trivial term as an error.

ties.name: Deduction.ch_balance
ties.plain: The exact count identity from character orthogonality

rows.name: Deduction.ch_balance
rows.plain: The exact count identity from character orthogonality
rows.note: For an eligible host, subtracting the explicit main term from the weighted prime-power count gives an exact combination of smoothed character prime sums. The compiled proof uses this identity in the form that takes a finite set of primes in place of the earlier version’s pair of primes.
rows.annotation: In the older identity the two primes $2,q_1$ have their inertia and Frobenius in $\Phi$; in `ch_balance` this is required throughout $S$. The count itself has the same definition. Indeed, for $p\in S$, the character sum at $p^i$ is supported on $i\operatorname{Frob}_p+I_p$ (in additive notation), which lies entirely in $\Phi$; there is no contribution to the sum over $g\notin\Phi$, even if $p$ ramifies in the host. Thus no new term has to be added to ASK when the fixed character of a level requires further ramified primes.

ties.name: Deduction.ch_core
ties.plain: A near-square-root bound for the kept characters’ weighted sum

rows.name: Deduction.ch_core
rows.plain: A near-square-root bound for the kept characters’ weighted sum
rows.note: Under the host and size hypotheses, a bound for the prime-power count at each translate controls the weighted sum over kept characters by $x^{1/2+(C+3)\varepsilon}$ plus the sum of the absolute values for omitted characters. The compiled proof uses this estimate to bound the growth of the character sums at each level.
rows.annotation: In `GrowthInequalityForm` the average is over all of $H$ and the three non-trivial characters of $(\mathbb Z/2)^2$ must already have small sums at $x$, leaving an estimate for $G$ alone. In `ch_core` one averages instead over $A_0\subseteq H$, so characters trivial on $A_0$ but not on $H$ can survive. Among these surviving characters one keeps a set $\mathcal K'$ of characters trivial on $\sigma$, with weight $1$ on those trivial on $H$ and $\beta$ on the others; the latter weight comes from the average on $TT$. This yields the one-sided estimate of Statement 4.3 for the kept sum, with the absolute values of the other surviving sums as an error. The new form can therefore treat a level of Dirichlet characters together rather than just the zeta function.

ties.name: Deduction.CH.HostFactsS
ties.plain: Ramification and splitting conditions on the host

rows.name: Deduction.CH.HostFactsS
rows.plain: Ramification and splitting conditions on the host
rows.note: The compiled proof uses this host record to impose trivial inertia outside a finite set $S$ and a distinguished prime $d$. At primes in $S$, both inertia and Frobenius lie in the index-two subgroup that defines the CM type. At $d$, the inertia group has order two with a specified generator.
rows.annotation: The conditions on $S$ are splitting conditions in the quadratic field fixed by $\Phi$, not complete splitting in the host: both the inertia group and the Frobenius class have trivial image in $\mathfrak G/\Phi$. This distinction is needed in [Section 9.1](pdf#subsection.9.1), where primes of the conductor of a fixed character may ramify in the host but split in $\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-d})$. Formally `HostFactsS` requires $2,q_1\in S$, $d\notin S$, trivial inertia at primes outside $S\cup\{d\}$ and inertia $\{0,\sigma\}$ at $d$. It is a condition on the given inertia and Frobenius data; the existence of hosts with those data is a separate step.

ties.name: Formalism.MainNotions.G.gainP
ties.plain: The explicit gain at a prime

rows.name: Formalism.MainNotions.G.gainP
rows.plain: The explicit gain at a prime
rows.note: The linked definition supplies the local divisibility gain for each prime and lift in the compiled RH argument, by summing the gains over Frobenius orbits and returning zero in the excluded cases. The three namesakes mentioned here live in other namespaces and sit outside the final dependency cone.
rows.annotation: The name meant in Section 5.3 is `Formalism.MainNotions.G.gainP`. At a fixed prime $p$ and lift $j$, its summand on an orbit is $\max(g_0,0)$, with the extra option $g_U-\mathrm{Pr}$ only on orbits in $VV$. The whole gain is set to zero at an inert prime with zero Frobenius step, or above the cutoff `X''`. These are gains before the word-dependent rescaling: in (5.1) one sums the retained gains and the signed corrections $\mathrm{fo}_j-\mathrm{ee}_j(u,\lambda)$ over the lifts. The three other declarations of the same short name are not the one used to define this gain.

ties.name: Formalism.DworkPowerSeriesWeights.thmBGauss
ties.plain: A Gauss-sum bound for paired jets

rows.name: Formalism.DworkPowerSeriesWeights.thmBGauss
rows.plain: A Gauss-sum bound for paired jets
rows.note: Lean proves an upper bound for the $p$-adic norm of every coefficient of a polynomial obtained by pairing products of minors with an integral-jet series times a quadratic exponential. The bound depends on the minor sizes and the selected positions. The theorem is outside the final dependency cone.
rows.annotation: There are two copies of the variables in Theorem B. Starting with a series $s$ whose jets $\kappa![X^\kappa]s$ are integral, one multiplies by $\exp(-S\sum_{t,a,b}u_t X_{t,ab}Y_{t,ab})$, with $|S|_p\le p^{1/2}$ and $|u_t|_p\le1$. In the simplest case $s=1$, $u_t=1$ and one pair of variables, the mixed jet of orders $a,b$ of $\exp(-SXY)$ vanishes unless $a=b$, when it is $(-S)^a a!$: only paired derivatives can cost a factor $p^{1/2}$ per pair. The theorem bounds each coefficient of the polynomial obtained from products of minor differential operators by $p^{D/2}$, where $D$ is the total height of first-copy minors, less their height-one count at top places, plus the count of second-copy minors at top places. This is a bound for possible denominators, valid for any prime, not the positive valuation estimate of Section 6.1. The theorem `thmBGauss` is proved in the archive but is outside the cone.

ties.name: Formalism.L2.KerInert.JetsInert
ties.plain: Integral theta-kernel jets at inert primes

rows.name: Formalism.L2.KerInert.JetsInert
rows.plain: Integral theta-kernel jets at inert primes
rows.note: This proposition asserts integrality of the theta-kernel jets for admitted lattices at inert primes $p\ge 5$. Lean derives it under auxiliary hypotheses on the local model and bases. The compiled RH proof uses kernel integrality and a separate jet bound to obtain divisibility of the periods.
rows.annotation: The two statements have the same outer hypotheses on the CM curve, character, inert prime and admitted lattices. `IntInert` says that after substitution of the formal logarithm in an orthonormal local basis and multiplication by the correcting exponential the coefficients of the resulting series are integral; `JetsInert` requires the original series to satisfy the integral-jet condition `JetsInt`. There is a theorem `jetsInert_of_int` deriving the latter from the former given `CM2`, existence of the orthonormal basis and integrality of the correction jets. For the gain of [Section 6.2](pdf#subsection.6.2), however, the integral power series is itself useful: the height-two logarithm and the estimate for the exponential give a lower bound for the jet valuations depending on the derivative orders, not just integrality. The proposition `JetsInert` is outside the cone.

ties.name: Formalism.RankGapBounds.WeightedMeanData.Data.MeanBoundSecondForm
ties.plain: An alternative upper bound on the mean count

rows.name: Formalism.RankGapBounds.WeightedMeanData.Data.MeanBoundSecondForm
rows.plain: An alternative upper bound on the mean count
rows.note: This proposition bounds the mean of the weighted prime-power count by the mean of its main term plus an explicit error built from the lattice and slope estimates. It is the second form of the mean bound and sits outside the final dependency cone.
rows.annotation: For each translate $u_0$ the slope comparison still uses the rank-weighted mean over words $u$. What changes in `MeanBoundSecondForm` is the next averaging: its hypotheses bound the ordinary means over $u_0$ of $\mathrm{ASK}-\mathrm{Ga}$ and $\mathrm{IO}$, and its conclusion is $\operatorname{mean}_{u_0}(\mathrm{ASK}-\mathrm{MAIN})\le\mathrm{ErrX}$. Such a bound is compatible with a large positive excess at a particular translate. In the form on the path, `LossBounds` bounds both losses separately at each $u_0$, and `each_unit_bound_statement`, with the other revised clauses, gives an error `ErrX5at` at that translate. It is this last form that supplies condition (3) of [Statement 4.3](pdf#theorem.4.3); the averaged proposition is not used.

ties.name: Formalism.B.DetGain
ties.plain: A determinant bound for log-prime-weighted gains

rows.name: Formalism.B.DetGain
rows.plain: A determinant bound for log-prime-weighted gains
rows.note: Let $\Delta$ be a nonzero integer determinant. If each local gain $g_p$ is at most the exponent of $p$ in $|\Delta|$, then $\sum_p g_p\log p\le\log|\Delta|$, with the sum over the specified primes. This product-formula estimate is outside the final dependency cone.
rows.annotation: This is the prime-factorisation argument for a single non-zero integer $\Delta$. If $p\nmid\Delta$, the condition forces $g_p\le0$; for primes dividing $\Delta$ the full budget is $\sum_p v_p(\Delta)\log p=\log|\Delta|$. Hence summing $g_p\log p$ over any specified finite set of primes costs at most this budget, without requiring $g_p\ge0$. The same elementary device explains the utility of one integer for all coefficient primes in the cohomological bounds below, but this particular proposition is outside the cone.

ties.name: Formalism.ThetaLiftIndependence.DetChain
ties.plain: Determinant factorisation for matched scalar blocks

rows.name: Formalism.ThetaLiftIndependence.DetChain
rows.plain: Determinant factorisation for matched scalar blocks
rows.note: Suppose several operators act by scalars on matching direct-sum blocks of equal dimension. If another operator acts on each block by $\kappa$ times the product of their scalars, its determinant is $\kappa$ raised to the total dimension, times the product of their determinants. This formulation is outside the final dependency cone.
rows.annotation: The spaces of the operators need not be identical. In `DetChain` write $E=\bigoplus_s E_s$ and $W_j=\bigoplus_s W_{j,s}$ with $\dim W_{j,s}=\dim E_s=d_s$ for every lift $j$. The endomorphism $A$ acts on $E_s$ by $\kappa\prod_j\lambda_{j,s}$, and $B_j$ acts on $W_{j,s}$ by $\lambda_{j,s}$; thus each factor occurs with the same multiplicity $d_s$ on the two sides of $\det A=\kappa^{\dim E}\prod_j\det B_j$. The identity does not assert that $A$ is a composite of the $B_j$. It has the shape of the determinant hypothesis of `BoundsMu` in [Section 5.5](pdf#subsection.5.5), but this proposition is outside the cone.

ties.name: Formalism.ThetaLiftIndependence.DetBlocks
ties.plain: Determinant of an operator scalar on each block

rows.name: Formalism.ThetaLiftIndependence.DetBlocks
rows.plain: Determinant of an operator scalar on each block
rows.note: If an operator acts by a scalar on each summand of a direct sum, its determinant is the product of those scalars raised to the dimensions of their summands. The declaration records the block calculation behind determinant factorisation and sits outside the final dependency cone.
rows.annotation: If $E=\bigoplus_s E_s$ and $A$ acts as $c_s$ on $E_s$, a basis formed by joining bases of the $E_s$ has $c_s$ on the diagonal $\dim E_s$ times. This gives $\det A=\prod_s c_s^{\dim E_s}$, the assertion `DetBlocks`. The exponent is the dimension of the block, not the number of blocks; no diagonalisation theorem or non-vanishing assumption on the scalars is needed once these internal direct sums and scalar actions are given. This proposition is outside the cone.

ties.name: PI.BesselPeriodGGP.BesselPeriodGGP
ties.plain: Bessel period nonvanishing under interlacing conditions

rows.name: PI.BesselPeriodGGP.BesselPeriodGGP
rows.plain: Bessel period nonvanishing under interlacing conditions
rows.note: For discrete-series and coefficient representations satisfying the stated interlacing and half-integrality conditions, this proposition asks for translates of the lowest vector giving a nonzero Bessel-period integral. The named nonvanishing statement sits outside the final dependency cone.
rows.annotation: This is a local non-vanishing statement for the indicated discrete series $\sigma$ and the finite-dimensional type $\pi$, with $k$ even, $u_i>v_i>u_{i+1}$, the terminal inequality $u_{k-1}>-b_0$, and half-integral differences of the parameters. For each lowest unit vector $w$ and the prescribed Haar measures it asks for two group elements $x_0,x$ such that the integral of $\langle\sigma(x_0)w,\sigma(hn)\sigma(x)w\rangle\overline{\psi(n)}\pi(h)^{-1}$ is a non-zero operator on the space of $\pi$. The translations are part of the conclusion, not arbitrary choices for which non-vanishing is asserted. In Section 7.2 the Bessel-model input is instead proportionality of two Bessel maps on smooth vectors under a large-gap condition (`UniqGap`); that is a uniqueness statement, not this existence statement. `BesselPeriodGGP` is outside the cone.

ties.name: UpperTheory.V.Af.NumberSp4
ties.plain: A congruence integer for GSp(4)

rows.name: UpperTheory.V.Af.NumberSp4
rows.plain: A congruence integer for GSp(4)
rows.note: This proposition asks for one size-controlled nonzero integer whose $\ell$-adic absolute value is at most the product of the $\ell$-adic absolute values of the differences between the Frobenius traces of admissible $\mathrm{GSp}_4$ representations and the Eisenstein trace. The proposition is outside the final dependency cone. The compiled proof uses a unitary-group congruence number.
rows.annotation: For weights $(e+1,e,1,0)$ the comparison trace is $p^{e+1}z_1+p^ez_2+pz_3+1$, where the $z_i$ are fixed $k$-th roots of unity. The statement `NumberSp4` asks for one non-zero integer $NN$ before the choice of coefficient prime $\ell\ne2,p$: its valuation bounds the sum of the valuations of the non-zero differences from that trace for a finite family of pairwise non-isomorphic admissible representations. The logarithmic size bound is $c\varphi(k)(M(e+1))^A\log p$. The alternative `NumberSp4Alt` has the same conclusion but takes `AdmRAlt` in place of `AdmR`, with different automorphy and local safety predicates. The rank-four congruence argument is used in obtaining `CountII` and `CountIII`; it is the first formulation that is excluded here.

ties.name: UpperTheory.V.Af.CongruenceNumberRankThree
ties.plain: A congruence integer for rank-three unitary representations

rows.name: UpperTheory.V.Af.CongruenceNumberRankThree
rows.plain: A congruence integer for rank-three unitary representations
rows.note: In the first $\mathrm{U}(3)$ formulation, one size-controlled integer bounds the sum of $\ell$-adic valuations of the Frobenius trace differences from an Eisenstein trace for every coefficient prime $\ell\notin\{2,p\}$. Lean derives this formulation under separate hypotheses, and the compiled RH argument uses the version with different admissibility conditions.
rows.annotation: For the imaginary quadratic field $K$ and $q=\mathrm N\lambda$, both versions use the same comparison trace $q^{-e}z+1+q^ez^{-1}$ and compare it with traces at inverse Frobenius. One fixes a finite Galois-stable family $(z_o)$ of roots of unity and chooses $NN\ne0$ before $\ell\ne2,p$ and the sets of representations; the logarithmic bound is $c|O|(N(e+1))^A\log p$. Thus the sum of the log-prime-weighted valuation bounds is at most $\log|NN|$. What changes in `NumberU3U_s` of [Section 8.3](pdf#subsection.8.3) is the class of admissible representations: the irreducible case is `Adm3U_s` (which adds `Unl` to `Adm3Alt`), and the case with a trivial summand is `Adm2A` instead of `Adm2`. The same two predicates occur in `OneCharU_s`, which uses the trace comparison to bound a cohomological length. The older `CongruenceNumberRankThree` is outside the cone.

ties.name: GlobalTheory.BigTop.lamLow_of_classicalTheorems
ties.plain: A lift scalar lower bound from classical theorems

rows.name: GlobalTheory.BigTop.lamLow_of_classicalTheorems
rows.plain: A lift scalar lower bound from classical theorems
rows.note: Lean derives a lower bound on the theta-lift scalars from seven inputs, including the unitary Siegel–Weil formula and the doubling method. The compiled proof uses a different derivation whose doubling-method hypothesis is formulated through local zeta integrals.
rows.annotation: The scalars in question are those of the individual lifts: a lower bound for their logarithms gives an upper bound after subtraction in the period ledger of Section 5.5. Both derivations establish the eventual weight-size conditions and use `hookLogSum_sub_sizeTerm_le_lowerBound`, which gives the leading hook-product estimate used there. But `lamLow_of_classicalTheorems` concludes `LamLow` using `DoublingMethod`, whereas the theorem on the path, `lamLow_of_hypotheses_alt_alt`, concludes `LambdaLowerBound₂` using `DoublingMethodLocalZetaIntegrals`; the six other literature hypotheses are unchanged. It is the earlier derivation, not the use of the scalar estimate and the doubling method, that is outside the cone.
